#4777. Eli teases the launch of a much faster electric microcar

Eli Electric Vehicles is getting ready to reveal a new version of its tiny electric microcar, and this one could expand its usefulness beyond the slow lane.

In an Instagram teaser ahead of EICMA in Milan, the company announced the upcoming Eli ZERO MX, describing it as a new L7e vehicle joining its lineup. Eli also teased a special Race Edition, with promotional artwork showing a dark, sporty-looking ZERO with red accents and a visibly open-sided cabin.

The teaser doesn’t give us much to go on in terms of hard and fast details, but the L7e designation is the biggest clue here.

The familiar European Eli ZERO that we test-drove a few years ago is an L6e light quadricycle, with a top speed of 45 km/h (28 mph). Its compact two-seat layout makes it an appealing urban runabout, though that speed ceiling limits its usefulness on faster roads. But L7e vehicles can typically travel at speeds of up to 80-90 km/h (50-56 mph).

A faster version could make the little EV practical for considerably more trips. And there’s already a tantalizing hint: Eli’s Italian website lists an L7e ZERO capable of 85 km/h (53 mph), with a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles). Whether those specifications directly describe the upcoming ZERO MX remains unconfirmed by the teaser.

If they do, that would suggest a much more versatile commuter while retaining the tiny footprint that makes these vehicles so easy to park.

I like the idea of a faster LSV, maybe able to cruise at 40 mph. Not a good idea for freeways but suitable for almost all urban and suburban streets. For some a better option than a bike as an urban or second vehicle.

The Race Edition raises a different set of questions. The new vehicle could feature a sportier design, such as race seats and alternative doors. That could point toward a playful or more tuned vehicle, though we’ll have to wait to learn whether “Race” means additional performance or primarily a styling package.

It’s also unclear how closely the Race Edition and ZERO MX are related. The caption presents them separately, while the artwork additionally points towards a second-generation ZERO.

Either way, a roughly 50 mph Eli would be an interesting proposition: still small enough to rethink how much vehicle a daily commute requires, but potentially fast enough to cover routes the original couldn’t comfortably handle.

Eli says the reveal takes place at EICMA, November 3–8, in Hall 22, Stand B40. We’ll be there to see what they unveil.

#4775. 5 Surprising Findings From the Science of Happiness

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

The Norwegian town of Tromsø is home to the usual delights of a typical northern European city, and a few others one might expect of a place 300 kilometers north of the Arctic Circle. For example, from late November to mid-January, the sun never rises here. At the nearby UiT The Arctic University of Norway – the world’s northernmost university – psychologist Joar Vittersø has been studying the science of well-being for over 40 years. I asked him whether the winter’s veil of darkness affects him. Yes, he said, positively.

There’s much to like about polar night season – the snow, the beauty, the coziness of a slower pace, the contrast with what will follow. And for the negative elements, there’s adaptation. In fact, that people continue to be surprised by how readily they get used to things is among Vittersø’s own biggest surprises. Another of his insights is about the process of scientific progress. Human nature reveals itself gradually and knowledge is accrued “stone by stone.” Thankfully, “there’s an infinity to knowledge,” always something new to discover. This is good news for all of us – it keeps the well of engagement, interest and hope perpetually full.

According to Vittersø, the shortest definition of well-being is to like one’s life. You have to like it hedonically, with all its joys and pleasures and satisfaction they bring, but also eudaimonically, for the opportunities it offers for growth and becoming a better person. And if the good life remains elusive, Vittersø thinks that might be partly due to our idealized fantasies of “true happiness” as something “extremely intense, rare and beautiful.” If that’s your idea, then you will be disappointed, he says, because emotions – whichever affective pole they lean towards – don’t last forever. Things are always in motion. Just like life under the northern skies of Tromsø, light and darkness take turns with their visits.

Here is Vittersø with five counterintuitive findings from the science of well-being.

This is surprising at first glance, but if you ask people how much sadness they would like in their perfect life, very few say zero – it’s somewhere between 1% and 5%. There are situations where happiness is simply not the appropriate response. We not only need negative feelings, but we also want them to some degree (but not too much). For example, we know that without one of the most intense negative feelings, namely pain, we wouldn’t survive. Pain is a signal that something is hurting us, and we need to deal with it. So, upon reflection, people realize that a good life is not the complete absence of negative feelings. We don’t only want happiness – we want a variety of emotions. Anything meaningful, like goals and relationships, requires effort and includes challenges.

Values are very complex. We have many of them, and we need them, but we can’t hold all of them in our attention at the same time. Thus, we organize them hierarchically, so that we can concentrate on particular values while doing our tasks. But if something else needs our attention – our child is crying or the fire alarm goes off – then the whole hierarchy reorders itself in a split second. I think that’s a very functional way for a mental system like the human brain to organize values: what matters most depends on the situation. It is important to remind ourselves about our values if we are tempted towards breaking them. Some values are moral: they oblige us to do things because they are right, not because they make us emotionally happy. I think the advice to “be true to your values” is about those we have reason to value – the values we agree about upon reflection. They are not necessarily identical to those that spontaneously come to mind.

When you ask people how satisfied they are with their lives, almost everyone can come up with an answer in a few seconds. Yet, we often struggle with simple everyday judgments, like which clothes to buy. But the notion of “life satisfaction” refers to an “all things considered” evaluation of your life as a whole, and surprisingly enough, we are able to make such judgments quickly and easily.

My theory is that this helps us survive. Judgements of good or bad come spontaneously, because we can’t stand there forever wondering whether a dangerous situation is good or bad. That capacity has evolved for a reason, and we are quite good at it. Life satisfaction responses resonate with many valuable things in life – but not all of them.

Over the last years, I’ve asked participants in at least 15 different samples: If you had to choose between being a morally good person and being satisfied with your life, which is more important for you? In every study, 80 to 90 percent say being a morally good person. But when we ask about how morally good you would be in your perfect life versus how good you actually behave, most people have a gap. And you would predict that a big gap between your ideal and your current life would reduce life satisfaction. It hardly does. Hedonic gaps, however, affect us strongly.

I think one explanation is that life satisfaction comes from a spontaneous good-bad evaluation, while morality is determined by a right-wrong rationality. Including it requires us to pause and reflect on what we mean by “goodness.” That is enough to keep morality out of the spontaneous judgment, even if you personally think of it as an important value.

The hedonic part of a good life is easy to measure but the eudaimonic elements are difficult. The essence of eudaimonia, to keep developing our human potential, doesn’t reveal itself easily in a survey. Yet, to understand the good life, we need both.

Many thanks to Joar Vittersø for his time and insights. Dr. Vittersø is Professor in Social Psychology at the Department of Psychology at UiT The Arctic University of Norway.

#4774. How Europe’s battery passport could have a big impact on US e-bikes

Europe is preparing to introduce a new requirement that could change how electric bicycle batteries are tracked, repaired, recycled, and potentially even resold. Starting in February 2027, new e-bike batteries sold in the European Union will be required to carry a digital battery passport, giving each battery its own digital identity and making important information about its origins and characteristics accessible throughout its lifetime.

And while the rules are European, their impact could eventually reach American e-bike riders, too.

The battery passport requirement comes from the EU’s 2023 Batteries Regulation, which established new standards for battery sustainability, traceability, and transparency. The rules cover several categories of batteries, including those used in electric cars, electric bicycles, electric scooters, and other light electric vehicles.

Beginning February 18, 2027, newly placed batteries in these categories will need digital passports accessible through QR codes. Scanning the code will provide access to information about the battery, though exactly what users can see will depend on their authorization level.

The information can include details such as the battery’s manufacturer, chemistry, capacity, cycle count, carbon footprint, and materials used in its construction. The system also provides for information about battery performance and durability, including data related to battery health and degradation.

That last part could be particularly interesting for electric bicycle owners.

Anyone who has purchased a used electric bicycle knows that the battery is often one of the biggest unknowns. A bike might look nearly new, but its battery could have hundreds of charge cycles under its belt and significantly reduced capacity.

Even a quick test ride before a secondhand e-bike purchase may fail to demonstrate just how little capacity remains in a heavily used battery.

With replacement e-bike batteries costing hundreds of dollars, that’s a pretty important detail.

The battery passport system could eventually help address that problem by making battery information more transparent. However, there’s an important distinction: the regulations don’t necessarily guarantee that everyday consumers will be able to scan a QR code and immediately see a battery’s remaining health percentage. Some of that information may be restricted to authorized users.

Even so, the system could help repair shops, recyclers, and secondhand buyers better understand the batteries they’re dealing with.

It could also make life more complicated for e-bike manufacturers, especially smaller brands that will now need to ensure their batteries meet the new documentation and traceability requirements.

There’s currently no equivalent nationwide battery passport requirement for electric bicycles in the United States, but that doesn’t mean American riders won’t eventually benefit.

I think it's really great that European consumer protection laws have a global impact because of the size of the European single market, and that they make life just a little bit easier for consumers all over the world. USB-C was just the beginning—there's more to come!

Many major e-bike manufacturers sell their products in both Europe and North America. US-based companies like Trek and Specialized have major markets in Europe, and will have to comply with the new law. Chinese companies and other Asian manufacturers will also need to produce compliant batteries. Once those companies have developed systems to track individual batteries and provide digital passports for their European products, they may find it easier to extend those systems to their American models rather than maintain entirely separate processes.

That doesn’t mean US-bound batteries will automatically receive passports, but it could create an interesting spillover effect.

And considering how expensive e-bike batteries can be, anything that makes it easier to understand their condition, verify their origins, or facilitate repairs could be a welcome development.

For now, Europe is leading the charge on battery transparency. But if the system proves useful, American e-bike riders might eventually get some of the same benefits without waiting for Washington to catch up.

#4773. Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

The researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she said.

Research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion said that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly important at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross said.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an important part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.

#4772. Your ‘Healthy’ Soda Alternative May Not Be So Healthy for Your Liver

WE'RE LONG PAST having to make a decision between just Coke or Pepsi. You've got a lot of options if you're bored of water—from fizzy nonalcoholic drinks to flavored seltzers. But while a lot of these drinks market themselves as healthy alternatives to sodas, research suggests they could be silently doing a number on your liver health.

If you've done the work to switch to diet sodas or have learned to love prebiotic sodas like Olipop or Poppi, the news can be pretty hard to hear. So it's important to get this out of the way upfront: If you have a "healthy" soda every once in a while, the experts we spoke to say the risk of having liver problems is unlikely. The real danger to your liver is if you’re tossing these back on a daily or near-daily basis. Here's everything you need to know.

THE STUDY PRESENTED at the United European Gastroenterology (UEG) Week 2025 used data from 103,251 people who enrolled in the UK Biobank and didn’t have liver disease at the start of the study. Participants were asked to fill out questionnaires about what they ate and drank throughout the day. The researchers then paid close attention to how much sugar-sweetened and low- or non-sugar-sweetened beverages they drank.

The major takeaway from the study is that it pretty much linked any drink that wasn’t water to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). You might know it by its former name, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). But whatever you call it, it's no joke.

MASLD happens when too much fat builds up in your liver from inputs other than alcohol. It can lead to serious liver scarring or end-stage liver disease. It can also put you at high risk for heart disease and diabetes. According to the American College of Gastroenterology, heart disease is the number one killer of people living with MASLD.

DAILY DRINKING OF nearly 9 ounces of any type of drink that was not water was associated with a significantly higher risk of developing MASLD. That risk jumped 50 percent for sugar-sweetened beverages and was surprisingly higher—60 percent—for those who drank low- or non-sugar-sweetened beverages. (Though some of these prebiotic sodas have more sugar and less fiber than marketing claims might imply).

After a 10-year follow-up, 949 people developed MASLD and 103 died from liver-related causes. Both types of beverages were significantly connected to increases in liver fat.

Replacing nearly 12 ounces of sugary beverages with water lowered MASLD risk by 14.4 percent and by 13.5 percent with low- or non-sugar-sweetened drinks. But if you switched completely from a sugary beverage like soda to a low-sugar beverage like fruit juice, the authors found that this did not help lower a person's risk of developing MASLD.

Exactly which beverages raised risk is hard to say because the authors did not directly state what low- or no-sugar drinks people were drinking. That said, there are lots of sodas that are marketed as being healthier alternatives that are not as good as they claim, according to Danbee Kim, MD, nutrition expert and assistant professor at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School.

“Even beverages marketed as ‘natural’ or ‘health-oriented’ may still fall into this category if they rely on sweeteners instead of sugar,” Kim says. “The key commonality is that they provide sweetness without significant calories. However, they may still affect liver health.”

A FEW THINGS may be going on here. “Low/non-sugar sweetened beverages, although low in calories, may still affect liver health through several pathways,” says Lihe Liu, a graduate student researcher at The First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University in China and lead study author. “They can alter the gut microbiome, interfere with feelings of fullness, increase preference for sweet foods, and in some cases stimulate insulin secretion.”

When you have something that’s sweet, even if it doesn’t contain much or any sugar, it sets off a chain reaction in your body the same way as if you were to actually have sugar, says Albert Matheny, RD, CSCS, registered dietitian and co-founder of SoHo Strength Lab. “You’re basically tricking your body,” he says. “Your body still reacts as if it has sugar.”

As a result, Matheny says your body produces more insulin (a hormone that helps regulate blood sugar), and encourages the liver to take in more sugar from your bloodstream. This can lead to metabolic disruption.

“Some artificial sweeteners may alter how the body handles glucose and insulin, contributing to insulin resistance, which is a key driver of metabolic dysfunction and fat accumulation in the liver,” says Kim. This process may even mess with your appetite, making you think that you're hungry when you're not.

Another reason has nothing to do with your gut, but with your mind. Kim says we can't discount the possibility that people who drink these low- and non-sugar-sweetened beverages may subconsciously compensate for the “saved” calories by eating more sugary or fatty foods later.

Keep in mind that all this is speculation. The explanation for why and how artificially sweetened beverages are linked to MASLD is still under investigation since Liu says her team didn't look too deep into this.

NOT NECESSARILY. “THEY’RE definitely an improvement over traditional diet sodas,” Matheny says. “That’s not to say that they’re a totally healthy option.”

When given a choice, water reigns supreme. And even then you still don't want to go too overboard.

If you still want to crack open a cranberry fizz prebiotic soda or even an unsweetened iced tea, Matheny says that’s probably fine, too. “In moderation, kind of everything is OK.”

#4771. Helping Your Child Get Started With Schoolwork

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Then you check your child’s grade portal and realize that homework and assignments are missing, or test grades look like there was never any real studying done. Does this pattern sound familiar?

For many families, getting homework completed or preparing for a test or quiz is not just an academic challenge but, rather, a daily struggle involving motivation, time management, initiation or getting started, planning, and follow-through. Parents become frustrated because their children seem capable of doing the work but struggle to get started. Children become frustrated because they feel nagged, overwhelmed, or misunderstood.

When executive functioning skills are still developing, telling a child to "just get it done" isn’t addressing the struggles. Instead, we need to help children learn how to get started, manage their time, work through resistance, and follow a plan, even when they would rather be doing something else.

Here are a few strategies to try with your child or teen:

Not every child is ready to tackle demanding work the moment they walk through the door after school. Many children and teens have spent the entire school day working hard to manage their attention, behavior, emotions, and social interactions. By the time they get home, they are mentally exhausted.

Rather than expecting your child, who has spent a ton of mental, physical, and emotional energy all day, to be able to jump right into their homework assignments, build in a break for your child or teen so he or she can decompress for one hour. A snack, movement, music, time outdoors, or a little quiet time may help them transition from school to home. Set a timer and, after one hour, take out school materials with your child or teen in one consistent space in your home, and review the assignments that need to be completed.

What you are doing is building in a time to disconnect from school, then reconnect in a calm way and tackle the assignments that need to be completed. The goal is to find the sweet spot when your child is most ready to engage in undesirable tasks that require attention and follow-through to get them done.

Executive functioning practice does not have to feel like another lecture. Our children can be more engaged when they can participate in a challenge, solve a problem, or compete against their own performance. On a separate pad of paper or a large or small whiteboard, have your child write down the assignments that need to be completed for the night. Then, ask your child or teen to predict how long an assignment will take to complete and write it down. For example, you can ask your child or teen, "How long do you think these 12 math problems will take?" Set the timer and let your child go. When the timer rings, your child can then see how accurate he or she was about the duration of the assignment. If she finishes before the timer, awesome! If he needs more time, estimate how much longer based on how many problems were completed during the time frame. Set the timer again and go! Over time, your child or teen will be able to form a more realistic sense of how long an assignment will take to complete.

This process accomplishes yet another goal, and that is that it goes against the innately held idea that “My homework is gonna take forever!” This puts a time limit on homework assignments so that there is an end time. The goal is to finish the assignments rather than sitting at a desk or table for hours at a time with very little work actually completed.

Then number the assignments in the order to be completed. For example, will he want to start on the hardest assignment first? Will she want to start on the assignment that takes the shortest amount of time? Having a choice also helps initiation.

You can also turn planning into a challenge by encouraging your child or teen to get the work done so they can have downtime for the rest of the evening. Kids and teens alike are often surprised when a parent or executive functioning coach emphasizes the importance of downtime and the need for it. Ultimately, the focus is not on speed or perfection but, rather, on developing awareness, planning, and problem-solving.

When children struggle with executive functioning, parents often become the source of every answer. In all transparency, many parents don’t want this role. They don’t want to be aware of and on top of every aspect of their child’s life to create movement. How many times have you heard yourself, as a parent, say things like:

Although these directions may be reasonable, your child or teen is not learning how to come up with their own strategies, and then they are dependent on you to get homework and other daily tasks done. If you happen to forget to verbalize the instruction or order, then it doesn’t get done. That is also maddening for a parent and creates an environment that supports your child or teen’s responses of “I don’t know. You didn’t tell me.”

Instead, ask questions that encourage accountability and a sense of responsibility:

You can guide your child or teen without making every decision for them. If the plan is unrealistic, help your child evaluate it. If she becomes stuck, offer a hint or a choice. But whenever possible, allow him to do the thinking. The more opportunities children have to formulate ideas, test strategies, and reflect on the results, the more practice they have to use their executive functioning skills.

Remember this: You are building skills for life. Executive functioning development takes time, and our kids and teens need opportunities to practice planning, managing time, initiating tasks, and following through. We can provide structure, encouragement, and accountability, but we also need to leave room for them to think, try, make mistakes, and learn from experience.

#4770. After 471,625 miles, this Chevy Bolt is doing better than you think [video]

Wondering how long your new electric car might last? This 2019 Chevrolet Bolt EV is proving that electric vehicles can rack up miles with the best of them – and its owner is committed to taking it past the half million mile mark.

You’d think a 250,000 mile Ford Mustang Mach-E maintaining 92% of its battery life, a 360,000 mile Hyundai IONIQ 5 with 87% battery health still intact, and a half-dozen stories of Tesla Model S, 3, and Y ride share vehicles racking up six figures on their odometers later would do more to convince the slow adopters and doubting Thomases of the world that EV batteries are built to last. The good news is that the evidence keeps piling up, and this latest example of electric endurance is a good one.

On the Out of Spec Renew YouTube channel, the crew took in a 2019 Chevy Bolt EV – one of the most affordable new EVs you could buy in 2019 – that had more than 470,000 miles on the clock and 330,000 miles on its post-recall battery. That’s nearly half a million miles on the original electric motor, and it’s still got more to go.

Average gas car lasts ~150k miles. For sure requiring more maintenance to reach that mileage than an EV. Achieving ~500k on the original motor and over 300k on a battery is quite impressive.

Getting towards the 100k mile mark in both our EVs. Both feel like brand new and have required almost no maintenance - a fraction of what would be required with ICE. Look forward to hitting 200k and beyond in each. For the first time in over 30 years of driving, I don’t look forward to replacing our cars as they get over 100k miles - rather I look forward to the next 100k miles of driving.

Out of Spec Renew replaced the 2019’s battery pack that was experiencing serious battery faults and cell-voltage imbalances with a stable, lower-mile example from a 2017 model. Once it was up and in, they got the car powered up, programmed, and driving again, putting the owner on track to reach the 500,000 mile milestone (sorry) in their trusty steed.

The OOSR crew paid $1,800 for the “new” battery, but estimates consumers would pay between $2,500-3,000 for the a similar pack. You can check out the full battery replacement video, below, then let us know how far you plan on taking your EV in the comments.

#4769. This 4-Week Workout Program Uses Just 1 Dumbbell to Help You Get Stronger

Build muscle and fry fat over this month-long workout plan.

YES, YOU CAN work every muscle in your body with one piece of gear. We love kettlebells, med balls, and resistance bands, but if we had to choose one piece of equipment, it would be a single dumbbell.

The game plan: Three times a week, you’ll grab the simplest tool in the gym and use it to build muscle and banish fat in a super-dense half-hour workout. It’s the most effective way to fry body fat, and it’s the perfect way to train for the holidays. It’s also exactly how Hollywood-based trainer Ben Bruno, C.F.S.C., guides time-strapped A-listers like Justin Timberlake and NBA star Klay Thompson. “They want quick, efficient workouts that hit everything,” Bruno says. “So we need to move fast.”

It doesn’t get more efficient than this light-speed, one-dumbbell workout.

Stand holding a dumbbell at your left shoulder, feet shoulder-width apart, knees slightly bent, glutes squeezed, and core tight. Keeping your chest level, straighten your arm to press the dumbbell overhead (b). Pause, then slowly lower the dumbbell back to your shoulder. That’s 1 rep; do 8 per arm.

Stand holding a dumbbell at your chest. Tighten your core and step back about three feet with your right leg. Keeping your chest up and the dumbbell high, bend your knees and lower your torso until your left thigh is parallel to the floor. Your right knee should be a few inches from the floor. Pause, then push off your right leg and stand back up. That’s 1 rep; do 10 per leg.

Eb says: Squeeze your glutes when you stand up. This will help you avoid lower-back pain when doing lunges.

Set a bench to a 45-degree angle and position yourself so your chest is against it; squeeze your abs and glutes. With your left arm out at shoulder height, hold a dumbbell in your right hand, arm hanging naturally. Squeeze your shoulder blades. This is the start. Keeping your shoulders and hips steady, row the dumbbell to your right hip. Pause, then return to the start.That’s 1 rep; do 10 per arm.

Eb says: This is more than a back move; your glutes and abs should be into it, too. Tighten them up so your torso doesn’t tip down to the side of the weight.

Lie on your back, holding a dumbbell in your left hand, arm straight, directly over your chest. Press your lower back into the floor and lift your legs slightly off the floor; lift your shoulder blades slightly, too. This is the start.Bend at the elbow and shoulder, lowering the dumbbell to your chest without losing torso position. Press back to the start. That’s 1 rep; do 8 per arm.

Eb says: Struggling with the position? Bend your knees to make it easier.

Lie on your back, knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Lift your right foot off the floor and tuck your right knee toward your chest. Tighten your core. Driving your left heel into the ground, push your lower back off the floor; squeeze your left glute as you do this. Pause, then return to the start. That’s 1 rep; do 10 per side.

Set up in pushup position, glutes and abs tight, right hand gripping a dumbbell. Squeeze your shoulder blades. Pull the dumbbell off the floor, rowing it toward your rib cage but keeping your hips and shoulders square. Pause. Return the dumbbell to the start. That’s 1 rep; do 8 per arm.

Eb says: Focus on flexing the oblique on the rowing side as hard as you canto keep your hips level.

This article was originally published in 2019.

#4768. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

#4767. Bestselling US e-bike Lectric XP4 relaunched in limited-edition with new colors and gear

The Lectric XP series has become something of an institution in the American electric bicycle market. As the country’s best-selling e-bike lineup, it’s helped put hundreds of thousands of riders on two wheels, largely thanks to its combination of affordable pricing, impressive performance, and practical features. It’s become the go-to electric bike in the US, but that hasn’t made Lectric complacent. Instead, the company is continuing to innovate.

Now, Lectric is giving its flagship XP4 a fresh makeover with three new limited-edition versions, each sporting a unique color and a new collection of accessories and upgrades designed for different types of riders, from urban assault roles to conquering your favorite off-road fishing spots.

The new Lectric XP4 Limited Editions come in three flavors: District, (black) Jubilee (pink), and Ridge (green). Each is priced at $1,399 and includes a 750W motor, upgraded accessories, and a distinctive matte paint job. That’s just a $100 premium over the existing XP 750, yet comes with a whole new host of accessories designed specifically for each special edition model.

So while the underlying bike remains largely unchanged from the bones of the XP 750, the new packages are designed to make the XP4 even more useful straight out of the box.

The District edition is aimed squarely at urban commuters, sporting a stealthy Matte Black finish and an accessory package designed for daily transportation.

That includes two waterproof pannier bags, a redesigned LevelUp rear cargo rack, a heavy-duty bike lock, and an upgraded high-output headlight. There’s also a fast charger, suspension seat post with comfort saddle, and handlebar phone mount.

It’s essentially a ready-made commuter setup, particularly for riders looking to replace some of their car trips with an e-bike.

The Jubilee edition takes a more casual approach, arriving in a distinctive Matte Thistle colorway. Designed for neighborhood cruising, weekend errands, and trips to the local farmers market, it swaps the commuter-focused panniers for a front and rear cargo package and a small roll-top bag.

It also includes the upgraded headlight, lock, fast charger, suspension seat post, comfort saddle, and phone mount.

Finally, the Ridge edition is built for riders who prefer their adventures a bit farther from the pavement.

Finished in Matte Forest green, the Ridge comes with front and rear cargo accessories for carrying outdoor gear, plus a fishing rod holder on the High-Step version. The Step-Thru model instead receives a weather-resistant roll-top bag.

Like the other two editions, the Ridge also includes the upgraded lighting, lock, charger, and comfort accessories.

“We wanted to deliver ready-made, purpose-built setups that empower our community to jump on and ride without having to configure their gear from scratch,” explained Lectric co-founder and CEO Levi Conlow.

Conlow also seems particularly proud of the new finishes, calling them the three best paint jobs Lectric has produced in its seven-year history.

While the new colors and accessory bundles are the main attraction, the bikes retain the same core features that helped make the XP4 such a popular choice.

That includes Lectric’s in-house developed dynamic torque sensor, which measures how hard the rider pedals to deliver a more natural-feeling electric assist experience.

The bikes also feature hydraulic disc brakes, an 8-speed Shimano Altus drivetrain, and a full-color TFT display.

As with the standard XP4, riders get the familiar folding frame design, integrated turn signals and brake lights, and 20-inch puncture-resistant mixed-terrain tires.

All three limited editions are available in both High-Step and Step-Thru frame configurations.

At $1,399, the new models aren’t trying to reinvent the XP4 formula. Instead, they’re offering a more fully equipped version of a bike that has already proven itself with American riders.

And that’s probably a smart move. Lectric has built its reputation on delivering an impressive amount of e-bike for the money, and bundling useful accessories into a relatively affordable package plays right into that strategy.

The limited-edition models are available now, though Lectric says quantities are strictly limited.

For riders who have been considering an XP4 but wanted something a bit more distinctive than the standard colors, these new editions could be a compelling reason to finally pull the trigger.

And for those looking to score an even better deal, Lectric has also officially kicked off its Black Friday sale.

The company is calling it its biggest sale of the year, with some of its lowest prices ever and discounts of up to $800 across its lineup.

So whether you’re eyeing one of the new limited-edition XP4 models or another e-bike in Lectric’s extensive catalog, now could be a particularly good time to buy.

#4766. Helping Your Child Navigate Emotions When You're Overwhelmed

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

We’ve all been there. Your 4-year-old can only find one of their spaceman boots and is in total meltdown; your middle schooler begs not to go to school because they’re convinced they have no one to sit with at lunch; your teen has stormed off when you simply asked if they started their homework. Meanwhile, you are just trying to make it through the finish line of the day. Somehow, it’s not looking good.

Our overwhelm meets their distress. It’s a stressful emotional gridlock.

Our overwhelm often comes from feeling like we have to change course: Do an abrupt swerve to stop or fix what our kids are feeling. And of course, it’s not like our kids don’t want that, but it’s not like that’s all they want either. Witness how, when we make a beeline for solutions, kids often respond with: “You don’t understand! You’re just trying to fix it! You never listen to me!”

But rather than whisking them away from their feelings, our best move is to go toward their emotions with them.

What is the best way for kids to process their emotions? I have created a process I call the Seven Shifts, and it works for any age—parents and kids alike.

The Seven Shifts is a repeatable throughline for any emotional situation; it involves first honoring what you’re feeling so you can settle back into a more thoughtful (versus reactive) state, then toggling to what the feeling is pointing to: the need for us to do our good work—zoom in and understand what our thoughts are telling us, then zoom out to question interpretations and consider other possibilities that are more helpful and… true.

Shift 1: Empathize—don’t fight or fix the feeling; just make room for it

Notice how just saying to yourself: “I’m worried for my child, or even I’m frustrated and too tired, and that’s OK” allows your body to soften. You’re not fighting where you are. You aren’t saying you don’t care; your caring is not up for debate. You are validating your own experience—it’s a place where people land. Lots of people.

Same for your child: Instead of rushing to reassure or correct—get to what I call the “nodding head of agreement.” Your child sees that you see where they are: “This is really upsetting you. This is a lot you’re carrying. You really didn’t want it to be like this.” It’s not about agreeing with the logic; it’s accepting without judgment—this is where your child has landed.

Often in a blur of competing feelings, we feel lost—and when we feel lost, we spiral. The antidote? Just start naming the feelings—there may be several, and they may seem like opposites—like loving and frustrated. They are what I call “Emotion Neighbors”—opposites can sit side by side and not add up: feeling frustrated and sad, hopeful and exhausted.

Kids may not be able to name their feelings—ask: Does it feel mad, like something isn’t OK with you, or more hurt, like something is missing?

Shift 3: Settle inside—slow down and reset

The body registers all the stress of our thoughts. Tiny resets, a big exhale, a sigh, help you shift out of crisis mode and into connection. Bringing your calm to your child helps them find their calm, too. Sometimes it’s invisible—just your slow breathing helps them find their calm. A regulated nervous system is the foundation of everything that follows.

What are the thoughts underneath the feelings? When we can find those gems—not necessarily positive—they tell us what we’ve been telling ourselves; knowing the narrative we’re reading helps point to what we need to reinterpret. When thoughts operate freely under our awareness, we get stuck in spirals of fear, frustration, or helplessness. Ask your child: “What’s your brain telling you? What is the alarm, going beep-beep-beep, in your mind?”

Shift 5: Zoom out—prism it to see multiple perspectives

Now that we’ve unearthed those gems, hold them up to the light and get different perspectives—translation: the things we say to ourselves unchecked we’d never say to a friend in a similar situation. We can fact-check our beliefs and edit accordingly and encourage our kids to do the same.

Help kids get in the habit of what I call “second-opinion thinking”: What would they tell a friend in that situation? What would a friend tell them? What would a hero or mentor say? Notice you’re not saying: “You’re thinking the wrong thing.” It’s an invitation: “Those thoughts sound like what anxiety says; can we fact-check it and see what else is more true?”

Shift 6: Take action one small step at a time

Equipped with a newer, truer story, is there a step you want to take that could help—like allowing yourself a “time out” and coming back to your child when you’ve had a second to reset? Or reminding yourself of your child’s strengths rather than just focusing on what’s wrong?

With your child, ask: “What’s a step that you could try—approaching a fearful situation? Saying something assertive to a friend? Scheduling grief time every day?”

Shift 7: Take stock and give credit where it is due!

We are the heroes of our lives, and our successes are in the tiny moments—notice them, and give credit where credit is due. Help them notice the progress they are making—and the way they made it—especially when things are hard. That’s how they will know how to value the steps along the way, not just the great moments across the finish line.

When we allow ourselves to turn toward—not away—from our emotions, the seven shifts become a two-for-one route toward understanding. Kids gradually learn the way from our responses and increasingly trust that they’ll come out with a better understanding of themselves and the world on the other side of the journey.

Here’s to better emotional navigation all around.

#4765. How to Find Out If You Got the Measles Vaccine as a Kid

The US may lose its measles elimination status after multiple outbreaks in the past two years.

THE US is likely to lose its measles elimination status this week when the Pan-American Health Organization, part of the public health arm of the United Nations, meets to review data from the multiple outbreaks that have occurred nationwide in the past two years.As of early November, there are 5,182 confirmed measles cases in 47 states. This is more than double of cases in 2025—the CDC reported 2,289 measles cases in 45 states. And a far cry from when measles were practically eliminated in the US with a record low of 86 cases two decades ago.

Of all the US cases this year, 96 percent come from people who are unvaccinated. Since most of us got the MMR (measles, mumps, and rubella) vaccine as a kid, it wouldn't hurt to double-check that you're protected against one of the most contagious infectious diseases in the world.

Now, there's no central repository of childhood vaccine records in the United States, says Brian Labus, PhD, MPH, assistant professor of epidemiology and biostatistics at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. So you'd need to find your copy of your vaccination records or get them from your pediatrician's office—which may or may not still be operating. There are a few other places to do that detective work (more below).

In lieu of that, some people are getting blood tests to check if they have antibodies for some of the diseases children are vaccinated for, but there are pros and cons with those. Here's what to know about making sure you're protected against measles and whether you got other vaccinations on the childhood immunization schedule.

IF YOU WERE born before 1957, it’s assumed that you were exposed to measles as a child and don’t need to be vaccinated, Labus says. If you’re around 45 or older, you were likely exposed to chicken pox and don’t need that vaccine, adds Thomas Russo, MD, chief of the division of infectious diseases at the University at Buffalo. There aren’t specific age cutoffs for other diseases, though.

But there is a blood test, called an antibody serology test, that can tell you if you have antibodies against certain diseases, including measles, mumps, chicken pox, hepatitis, tetanus, HIV, mononucleosis, and others.

These blood tests can suggest whether you’ve been previously infected with these diseases or vaccinated against them, Dr. Russo says. “The presence of antibodies indicates that your body mounted an immune response against a pathogen either due to a natural exposure or to a vaccination,” Labus explains. “It can also give you an idea about the level of protection you have in your body.”

While that generally means that you’re immune, it’s also not a guarantee, says Georges Benjamin, MD, executive director of the American Public Health Association. Also, antibodies decline over time.

Starting with an antibody test to determine your vaccination status might make sense for some people, but Labus says there are some practicalities to consider.

For one, the tests can be expensive, costing around $250, Dr. Benjamin says. Your insurance may or may not cover them.

It can also take several days to get the results. Labus says if you’re using the test to determine if you need a vaccine quickly, you’re potentially not protected during that wait. “While this doesn't matter for routine situations, it could be the difference between getting measles or avoiding it if you live in a community experiencing an outbreak,” he says.

If you're not sure you were vaccinated, Labus and the other doctors we spoke to suggest just getting the MMR, polio, DTap (diphtheria, tetanus, and acellular pertussis), and other shots just to be safe (more about that below).

But if you're not sure you want to get jabbed, your pediatrician retired long ago, and you have a moment to invest in detective work on your records, here's where to look:

• Old records you or your parents have at home, like a baby book.

• Any schools you attended. Many states require certain vaccines before you start kindergarten, including MMR, polio, DTap, and varicella, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. If you were in the military, you would have been required to get certain vaccines.

• The health department where you grew up. Some state health departments keep immunization records, Dr. Benjamin says. But whether yours are there may depend on your age. “State immunization registries are a relatively new development, and those systems were not likely in place when you were young if you are more than 25 or 30 years old,” Labus says.

TALK TO YOUR doctor about your concerns and uncertainty about your childhood vaccination status and level of protection against diseases, and they can suggest whether just getting the vaccine for the first time or a booster is appropriate, Labus says. “Most vaccines can be given to adults without any problems.”

Getting the shot is usually cheaper and faster than an antibody test, he adds. Dr. Benjamin points out that boosters are a good idea to consider especially if you have chronic diseases, immune system dysfunction, or work in the healthcare industry. Also consider it if you plan to travel to parts of the world with higher instances of diseases like measles, such as countries in the Middle East, Dr. Russo adds.

And by the way, even if you did get all your vaccines as a child, you still need to get a DTap or Tdap booster every 10 years as an adult for protection against diphtheria and tetanus, Dr. Russo says.

For the other childhood vaccines, “receiving an extra dose is going to boost your antibody levels even if you have previously been vaccinated, which is a good thing,” Labus explains. Dr. Russo agrees: “The path of least resistance is when in doubt, there’s no harm in getting a booster shot.”

#4764. Electric trucks hit 50% of China’s heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls

Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.

And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.

In 2024, new-energy vehicles accounted for 13.6% of heavy trucks (12 tonnes and up) sold in China. In 2025, sales nearly tripled to 231,100 units, up 182%, for a 28.9% share.

December 2025 hit 53.9%, but that was a rush. Buyers piled in before trade-in subsidies expired and new purchase tax costs kicked in, and the share dropped back to about 23% by March.

Then it came right back. Through the first nine months of 2026, China sold 226,400 electric heavy trucks, up 64%, for a 38.1% share. That’s already almost as many as in all of 2025, with a quarter still to go. In tractors, the big rigs that pull long-haul trailers, the September share hit 64.5%.

That’s well ahead of Beijing’s own plan. This year, 11 government bodies set a target of 40% new-energy heavy-truck sales by 2030, along with 1.6 million of them on the road, 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors and about 3,000 charging and swap stations. The market blew past that sales target four years early on a monthly basis, and CATL now says new-energy trucks will be half of China’s annual truck sales by 2028.

It comes down to cost. In most uses, an electric heavy truck in China is now cheaper to own and run than a diesel one, and fleets run that math every day.

CATL claims savings of about 0.6 yuan per km. Independent numbers are more measured, but still favorable: a study by the ICCT and China’s CATARC found battery-electric trucks about 19% cheaper per tonne-km than diesel in good conditions, though they lose that edge at low annual mileage or when battery weight eats into payload.

Charging time is the other objection, and China’s answer is swapping. CATL’s Qiji brand operated about 300 heavy-truck swap stations at the end of 2025 and plans 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 in 2027. In August, it agreed to pay 2.56 billion yuan (about $370 million) for nearly 25% of Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-truck swap operator with more than 1,600 charging and swap stations. Its new standardized packs hold 432 kWh and 513 kWh and swap in about five minutes.

CATL is already taking the swapping model to Europe with Octopus Energy.

The trucks themselves are domestic. XCMG led the segment in 2025 with a 15.4% share, ahead of SANY and FAW Jiefang, and the top three held 42.9% of the market. CATL supplied 60% of the batteries.

For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas. LNG trucks took nearly 30% of the market in 2024, when gas was much cheaper than diesel.

Now they’re losing to batteries. According to Kpler, LNG trucks had a 37% share of heavy-duty registrations in March, against 23% for electric. By July, electric was at 47% and LNG had collapsed to 11%. Monthly LNG truck registrations fell from more than 30,000 to about 6,200.

So China is skipping the “bridge fuel” phase for trucks almost as fast as it started it.

China’s diesel consumption already peaked. Rhodium Group found that diesel refinery runs topped out in April 2023, and apparent consumption dropped from 4.7 million barrels per day then to 4.0 million barrels per day in April 2025.

2026 is the steepest drop yet. Kpler estimates diesel demand fell about 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in May, roughly 10%, and 460,000 in June. It expects a decline of about 230,000 barrels per day for the full year and only a 64,000 barrel-per-day rebound in 2027.

Kpler puts the gross diesel displacement from alternative trucks at about 680,000 barrels per day this year: roughly 450,000 from the LNG fleet built in recent years and 230,000 from electric trucks. Road freight still grew about 3% through July. China is moving more goods with less diesel.

There’s a catch. The fuel price spike this spring, tied to the Iran war, cut demand on its own and pushed more fleets toward electric. But that only explains part of it, and the fleet is still early: electric trucks will be only about 8% of China’s heavy trucks on the road by the end of 2026, according to Kpler. Every year of 40-50% sales shares compounds the diesel losses.

Europe is growing fast from a tiny base. ACEA data shows 5,120 heavy electric trucks (16 tonnes and up) registered in the EU through September, up 59.9%, for a 2.5% share. That’s up from 1.7% a year ago, but diesel still took 91.7% of all EU truck registrations.

A few countries stand out. Switzerland is at 24%, Norway 14.4%, the Netherlands 11.1% and Sweden 10.3%. Germany registered the most units at 1,722, but that’s only a 4.2% share.

The US doesn’t publish an official electric Class 8 sales figure, and that tells you something. The best indicator is the recent order for 2,500 Tesla Semis through ZET SCALE, which would roughly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. Against about 230,000 Class 8 trucks sold per year, the electric share is well under 1%.

Price is the big difference. The ICCT puts the median electric Class 8 tractor in the US at $411,200, against $172,500 for diesel. Federal tax credits for commercial EVs ended in 2025, and California shelved the rule that would have required fleets to buy zero-emission trucks.

This is the biggest under-covered story in the EV industry right now.

Everyone argued for years about whether electric semis could work. Range, weight, charging, cost. China settled it the boring way. It got the price of a battery-electric heavy truck close enough to diesel, built swap stations along freight routes, and let fleet operators do what fleet operators always do: pick the cheapest truck per kilometer.

And the result is showing up where it matters, in oil demand. Trucks are where diesel lives. Displacing a quarter of a million barrels a day in one year, with electric trucks still only around 8% of the fleet, means we’re still early on this curve.

The contrast with the US is hard to watch. America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification. But electric Class 8 trucks cost 2.4 times as much as diesel here, the federal incentives are gone, and the market is under 1%. The ZET SCALE order is real progress. But it came from shippers pooling their demand, and twe have yet to see these trucks get delivered.

China having a lot of phev and EV vehicles has helped with oil pricing around the world, more notably in the current american-caused oil crisis. It would be worse if they were all traditional powered cars and trucks.

Now to be clear, I'm not saying that it has made a massive impact or is even the only reason why the oil crisis isn't much worse, it's just one of a few steps China made to reduce the impact of the oil crisis. But going electric everywhere we can has a stabilizing effect when oil shocks show up

Europe at least has the regulation, and its best markets, at 10% to 24%, are roughly where China was in 2024 and 2025.

The question now is how long Chinese truck makers stay home. SANY and BYD already sell electric trucks in Europe, and CATL is building the swap network for them. If those trucks can come close to China’s pricing, how long can Western truck makers keep charging 2x diesel?

Diesel trucks aren’t the only thing batteries are displacing. At home, pairing solar with an EV or a home battery can cut your energy bills dramatically. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4763. This Guy Lost 54 Pounds and Got Absolutely Shredded in 6 Months

At 46, Austin Cowburn wanted to overcome injuries and get back to feeling his best. Here’s how he did it.

At age 46, Austin Cowburn felt his training was "directionless," and he started putting on weight. This former runner and marathoner wanted to overcome injuries and get back to feeling his best. Here’s how he did it.

RUNNING HAS ALWAYS been my go-to exercise; as a younger man I joined several running clubs, and even finished as even finished pretty high up in the 1995 New York Marathon. I spent weeknights and Saturday mornings on the track or in a swimming pool. Cardio is familiar to me, and as I grew up, I stuck with it. Looking back, I realize means I didn’t have the understanding and technique to really benefit from weight training.

After a couple of years of directionless training, plus two injuries and rehab, and a poor diet, I put on weight. That inflamed other, niggling injuries, which made me feel like I just wasn’t at my best. I felt sluggish; my favorite clothes didn’t fit as well, and the new ones seemed to be smaller than I expected. I wanted to get back into marathons, but to do that I need to get fitter, stronger, and healthier. So, I approached Ultimate Performance Manchester for help.

We started with fundamental stuff: monitoring and being consistent with my diet. I went from eating a lot of rich, calorie-laden food, eating it at all times of the day, to something much more sustainable. I’d enjoy a blended berry smoothie in the morning with protein, and three scrambled eggs with spinach in mid-morning. Mid-afternoon and evening, I’d eat lean-meat chili, mainly turkey mince, with lots of vegetables thrown in, including peppers and tomatoes, as well as rice. I also enjoyed a low-fat, high-protein yogurt in the evening mixed with banana, honey, or chia seeds. On the weekend, I could indulge in a nice steak.

We often forget how big an impact diet can have on mood, energy levels, and your ability to train hard and get the best from yourself. Changing what I ate really reminded me of the importance of a foundational diet.

I trained three times a week in the gym, usually from 8 a.m. to 9 a.m. I loved getting it done first thing in the morning, which really set me up for the day. I would also run four times a week. I really got my love for running back during this time: my distances increased, and I had no injuries. I didn’t even have aches and pains afterward. Training, losing weight, and fueling my body correctly really helped me regain my fluidity of motion.

It also helped with my energy levels and sleep. I felt mentally sharper, more productive and more creative. People told me that my skin was glowing. Everyone was extremely positive and kind in and out of the gym, complimentary, and really encouraging. My family was very proud and surprised with the results, and I felt like the very best version of myself.

In six months, I lost 24.6 kg (54 pounds), bringing my body fat percentage from 28.2% to 11.6%. I dropped from an extra-large to a medium. I’ve continued training, and now I’m eating more, and building muscle mass. I’m looking to sustain my gains and also increase the number of exercises I have in my toolbox.

It’s great to be able to say that more, better training has helped me avoid injuries. The more I trained, the more I wanted to, and my stamina has gone through the roof. I’m happier, more relaxed, and more motivated; I just feel better about myself.

I think anyone can do this, and if you’re on the fence about it, just go for it. Set clear goals and look for help, whether that’s a professional trainer or just a friend who’ll hold you accountable. You don’t have to change all at once; I’d recommend not putting too much pressure on yourself from session to session. Enjoy your exercises; make sure you rest and refuel correctly.

#4762. Lexus is taking a page from China for its next electric SUV launching in 2027

Toyota’s luxury brand Lexus is launching a new electric SUV in 2027, its first vehicle built in China in over two decades.

It’s official. Toyota is breaking from tradition, planning to develop and produce the new vehicle in China rather than its home market of Japan.

Lexus confirmed the new vehicle will be made at its new manufacturing plant in Jinshan, Shanghai, and will go on sale in 2027.

As the first Lexus factory built from scratch overseas, the company said the new plant will bring together its global manufacturing capabilities.

Toyota broke ground on the facility in June 2025, saying the new facility will unlock “Lexus speed” as it aims to keep pace with domestic brands like BYD. Construction was expected to be completed this past August, with the first vehicle scheduled to roll off the assembly line in the fall of 2027.

The first Lexus model will be an electric SUV, produced using advanced manufacturing methods such as gigacasting to reduce costs and speed up output.

The facility will be a cornerstone of Toyota’s comeback plans in China, where it’s struggled to compete with local brands.

Production capacity will be around 1,000 units per month in 2027 as Toyota ramps up to “tens of thousands” in 2028.

Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20% in China last month, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales than the year prior. The market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” Toyota said.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Lexus’ new Shanghai facility is wholly owned by Toyota, enabling it to produce vehicles in China through its joint ventures.

The new electric SUV will go on sale in China in 2027. Specific details, including battery, range, and prices, have yet to be announced.

As part of its “with China, for China, strategy, Lexus said it will “continue to use China as a source of innovation,” adding it will “deepen localization efforts” to bring classic models to the market that meet local needs.

Toyota joins the growing list of major OEMs that are already tapping, or plan to tap, China for its next-generation electric vehicles.

While in other global markets, Toyota is sticking to its “multi-pathway” strategy, which includes all powertrains from electric to ICE; in China, it’s being forced to adapt.

China is Toyota’s third-largest market, following the US and Japan. To stay competitive and turn things around in China, Toyota will rely more on local partners and suppliers.

Developing the new Lexus electric SUV in China first rather than Japan is significant given Toyota’s traditional ways.

Typically, it takes Toyota about four to five years to fully develop a new vehicle. In China, automakers are now building them in as little as two years.

Toyota, like many automakers at this point, is turning to China for new tech, batteries, production methods, and other EV components to keep pace.
