#4716. 2026 Gifts of the Year: Our editors have picked the best presents for anyone on your list

Updated Nov 1, 2026 3:42 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

A gift card isn’t a terrible present, but we believe you can do better. That’s why the editors here at Popular Science have put together this list of our favorite gifts of the year. We spend all year researching, testing, and covering products, so we know what we’re talking about. Even if you don’t end up grabbing one of these exact products, it’s a great place to start. Show them you know what they like and leave the gift cards for your nephew who you don’t really like that much.

Popular Science‘s sibling brands have also selected unique products for their own Gift of the Year awards. See their best-in-class gift selections for this holiday season at PCMag, CNET, Mashable, Lifehacker, and ZDNET.

Waterproof trail shoes usually look and feel too bulky and—let’s be honest—kind of nerdy. The Speedgoat 7 GTX keeps the regular Speedgoat 7’s supercritical EVA midsole and Vibram Megagrip outsole, then wraps them in a GORE-TEX Invisible Fit membrane and a recycled Cordura upper. It’s a lot of technical materials, but they’re wrapped in a design that actually looks cool with a pair of jeans. Toggle laces work with gloves on, there’s a loop for attaching gaiters (sold separately), and reflective details run all the way around for dark November runs. We recommend going up a half-size from your giftee’s typical number for a better fit.

This little device gives the gift of time that would otherwise be spent doomscrolling. Phone screen-time limits are easy to dismiss because the override button sits right under your thumb. Brick moves the override into another room. The $59 block has no battery, just an NFC chip. You pick the apps to lock in the free iPhone or Android app, tap your phone to the Brick, and those apps stay locked until you walk back and tap again. One Brick works with multiple phones, so a household can share it, and the app includes five emergency unlocks per device for real emergencies. It requires iOS 18 or Android 12 and later. Brick is also HSA and FSA eligible, which makes it a stocking stuffer you can buy with pretax money.

Insta360 made its name with 360-degree and action cameras, and the Luna Ultra is its first pocket gimbal camera, co-engineered with Leica. The main camera pairs a Leica Summicron lens with a 1-inch sensor that records up to 8K at 30fps, and a second telephoto camera on a 1/1.3-inch sensor handles zoomed shots and background blur. A three-axis gimbal keeps footage steady while you walk. The 2-inch OLED touchscreen pops off and works as a wireless monitor and remote, so you can frame a shot of yourself from across the room. It’s a serious content creation tool that’s fun to use, which is a rarity.

You don’t need a massive backyard to have a true outdoor pizza oven. The propane cooker weighs 26.4 pounds and measures 16.9 inches wide, yet Gozney rates it to reach 950 degrees Fahrenheit, which is more than enough to put a perfect char on a true Neopolitan style pie. Gozney’s lateral rolling flame wraps heat over the top of the pizza while a 12mm stone floor stores heat for the crust. An infrared thermometer makes a smart add-on gift, since the oven won’t tell you when the stone is ready. You’ll selfishly also probably get some free pizza out of it.

A 65-inch black rectangle is a lot of nothing to stare at when the TV is off. LG’s Gallery TV LX7B fills that space with art. The 4K Mini LED set has a matte screen that cuts reflections and a snow-white magnetic frame that snaps onto the bezel, and when it’s idle it can display pieces from LG Gallery+, a library of more than 5,000 works (some features require a Gallery+ subscription). It runs webOS 26 with Google Gemini built in. Whether the receiver is a film buff or a die-hard design enthusiast, this TV fits the bill.

This is a product we use every single day. The Theragun Mini Plus is Therabody’s smallest heated massage gun, and its attachment warms up to 131 degrees Fahrenheit across three heat levels. It has three speeds, two buttons, USB-C charging, and a travel lock that keeps it from switching on inside a gym bag. Therabody says heat plus percussion works three times faster than percussion alone, based on its own lab testing. You can run either therapy by itself, too. Don’t think this is only for hardcore gym rats. It’s great for people who just want to relax of even improve their sleep.

If you know a budding streamer or podcaster, this is a gift that grows with them. The Razer Seiren V3 Pro has both USB-C and XLR outputs, so it plugs straight into a PC now and into a mixer later when they upgrade their setup. It’s a dynamic mic with a 30mm cardioid capsule, a type that picks up less of a noisy room than most condensers. Onboard processing runs AI noise removal, a compressor, and a limiter on the mic itself, and Windows users can record 32-bit float audio through Razer Synapse. A tap-to-mute button, an RGB ring that shows mute and gain status, and an adjustable desk arm all come in the box.

The nightstand device, built for kids roughly 4 to 10, walks one child through morning, after-school, and bedtime routines a step at a time with visual prompts that work for kids who can’t read yet. It also handles alarm clock, sound machine, nightlight, and OK-to-wake duty. It has no camera or microphone, and kids can’t browse the web or download apps on it. Skylight sells it for $139.99, and the optional $39-per-year Buddy Plus plan adds rewards, timers, and read-aloud messages.

Fast wireless charging makes a magnetic battery pack hot, and heat makes phones slow their charging down. Anker’s fix in the MagGo 2 Pro is a tiny fan. The 10,000mAh pack charges at up to 25W over Qi2.2, and Anker says the fan keeps its back under about 97 degrees Fahrenheit while it works. Anker rates it to take an iPhone 17 Pro to 50 percent in about 25 minutes. A screen shows battery level and charging speed, a built-in stand props the phone up for in-flight movies, and the USB-C port refills the pack at 45W. It costs $109.99. Older phones, including the iPhone 15 Pro, top out at 15W.

Google hadn’t released a new standalone smart speaker since the Nest Audio in 2020. The Google Home Speaker is built around Gemini for Home instead of the old Assistant, so you can stack several requests into one sentence or correct yourself mid-command. It plays 360-degree sound from a 58mm driver, two of them pair with a Google TV Streamer for surround sound, and it doubles as a Thread border router and Matter hub. It costs $99.99 and includes six months of Google Home Premium, which adds Gemini Live and continued conversation. After the trial, Premium runs $10 per month.

A $20 smart plug makes a surprisingly good energy audit. The Shelly Plug Gen4 measures real-time power draw from whatever is plugged into it, so you can see how much that garage fridge or space heater actually pulls. It connects over Matter, Wi-Fi, or Zigbee, works with Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, SmartThings, and Home Assistant, and can run locally without touching the cloud. It handles loads up to 1,800 watts, with cutoffs for overheating, overcurrent, and voltage problems. Its built-in LED can change color to reflect current energy use. It costs $19.99 in black or white.

If you know someone constantly struggling to make work from the road work, the Sennheiser MOMENTUM 5 Wireless headphones are an audio oasis they will appreciate for years to come. The hybrid noise cancellation, 8-band graphic EQ, Snapdragon Sound, and other personalization features cut the noise and sculpt the sound, perfect for open-office escapees and in-control commuters. And a long-haul battery life delivers up to 57 hours of runtime, so playlists won’t run out somewhere over the Atlantic. Plus, the battery is user-replaceable, reducing e-waste and extending ownership. This is the perfect gift for music-loving control freqs.

Sonos isn’t the only way to fill a house with speakers that talk to each other. Denon’s redesigned Home lineup runs on HEOS, which can link up to 64 speakers across a home, and the three sizes scale with the room. The $399 Home 200 plays stereo from three tweeters and a 4-inch woofer. The $599 Home 400 adds two upward-firing drivers for Dolby Atmos Music, and the $799 Home 600 packs eight drivers, including dual 6.5-inch woofers, each with its own amplifier. All three take Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, USB-C, and aux. The stone and charcoal finishes look more like something from a furniture store than an electronics aisle.

The Bose LifeStyle Ultra Home Theater Set is perfect for homes that struggle with the volume of content and components. From the soundbar to the wireless satellites and subwoofer, everything is compact and design-conscious, perfect for a minimalist who doesn’t want to sacrifice expression. Bose SpeechClarity uses AI enhancement to make dialogue more audible without having to ride the volume constantly. CustomTune calibrates immersion to the room’s actual acoustics. And when it’s not movie night, stream music via AirPlay 2/Google Cast, no app required. Add more speakers later for a multiroom setup, making this a great gift for someone who wants to scale up a whole-home setup without sacrificing space.

#4715. BYD’s 3,000-hp EV crashes at about 280 mph — Watch the driver escape unharmed

BYD’s electric supercar delivers an insane nearly 3,000 hp from four electric motors. During a high-speed test, the Yangwang U9 Extreme crashed at about 280 mph, but the driver walked away unharmed.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme is a “dream car,” as BYD calls it, a souped-up, track-focused version of its electric hypercar.

After it became the world’s fastest production car last year, reaching a top speed of 496.22 km/h, or about 308 mph, BYD is attempting to beat it by breaking the 500 km/h (310 mph) mark.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme features the world’s first mass-produced 1,200V ultra-high-voltage platform and BYD’s e4 platform.

The quad-motor setup is the first in the world rated at 30,000 rpm, BYD said, delivering nearly 3,000 hp (3,000 PS) combined.

While BYD is preparing to attempt a run this month, the company shared a video of the Yangwang U9 Xtreme crashing in a violent high-speed test.

During the first run, it clocked over 350 km/h (217 mph), no problem. On the second run, it hit over 420 km/h (261 mph).

However, during the third run, BYD was attempting to reach over 450 km/h (280 mph) when the vehicle violently crashed into the guardrail and continued spinning out of control. You can see some of the footage from inside the vehicle.

BYD said that after a comprehensive medical exam, the hospital found the driver in good health with no serious injuries.

When I was still in law enforcement, we did some pursuit driving training and you learn a lot about the dynamics of a vehicle. It's amazing just how quickly and badly something can go wrong at just 100 mph let alone nearly triple that speed. The fact is that the average person can't drive to the max limits of a basic car like a Corolla let alone super cars.

Is it time to reign in the HP and speed wars? Do we need vehicles that can do 0-60 in less than 3 seconds? Unless these companies begin to require 40+ hour specialized training courses in order to buy/operate these high HP vehicles today, then maybe it's time to stop the silly push for more.

And BTW. No matter what the performance levels are of any cars today, I still feel that it would be smart to push legal driving age to at least 17 or 18 instead of 16 and make getting a DL harder to do with way more emphasis on driver's education training.

The vehicle’s high-strength carbon-fiber cabin also held up impressively despite the front and rear damage.

It didn’t take long for BYD to try again, reaching a top speed of 457.89 km/h (284.5 mph) on the next run. Jiang Gong, one of Yangwang’s riders, said he sees some leeway and believes it can break 500 km/h (310 mph).

At the end of the video, BYD said (translated into English), “The ultimate pursuit has no end; the summit will eventually be reached.”

#4714. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4713. The grossest thing you touch every day, according to science

Published Nov 1, 2026 5:02 PM EST

It’s probably not something you want to think about, but what do you think is the dirtiest thing you touch every day? If you commute via subway, you might suspect a stairwell handle or train pole as the most likely culprit. If you go from your house to your car to an office, maybe it’s the elevator button or the key fob you have to dig out of your bag. All very good guesses–you might even be tempted to pull out your phone and look up the correct answer.

“It might surprise people, but the dirtiest thing they encounter every day is their own cellphone,” says Caitlin Mangan, a Lab Manager for Gillson Sciences. “People take them everywhere with them, including the bathroom. They are touched thousands of times a day, without people cleaning them or washing their hands in between tasks.”

The University of Michigan’s Institute for Healthcare Policy & Innovation puts it this way: Your cellphone is 10 times dirtier than a toilet seat. Yeah, that’s pretty gross.

The frequency of contact contributes to that grossness. The study shows that, on average, people check their phones 47 times a day. And like your clothing and shoes, you carry your beloved phone through various environments of differing cleanliness levels. In fact, that subway pole may actually be cleaner than your iPhone.

“It depends on how often the areas are cleaned,” says Mangan. “For example, an office building door handle typically has less people touching it day-to-day, but because of that it might not be cleaned as frequently and therefore has a high risk of having germs. Whereas a subway pole that is cleaned daily and properly sanitized will have less germs to transfer.”

Cellphones have been known to carry skin bacteria like Staphylococcus and Streptococcus, as well as fecal bacteria like E. coli and Enterococcus faecalis. These bacteria can cause skin infections, strep throat, or gastrointestinal illnesses producing nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. You can help yourself by avoiding using your phone in the restroom, not placing it down on surfaces where germs likely lurk, and when speaking into it, not letting it touch your cheek or mouth.

Of course, you should also clean your phone with paper towels, alcohol, and cotton swabs whenever possible and follow the number one rule of germ spread prevention: Wash your hands frequently and thoroughly.

#4712. Does the Space Where We Deliver Therapy Matter?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Picture yourself trying to discuss your deepest anxieties with your therapist while a conversation about last night’s TV can be heard outside the door. How about attempting a therapeutic exercise in a room barely large enough for two chairs?

A number of therapists have raised concerns to me about the spaces in which they are expected to work.

Some report being expected to conduct telephone or online sessions in settings where conversations could be overheard by colleagues or others nearby. Others describe working in noisy buildings, sharing spaces with services that have very different needs, or using communal waiting areas, which can unsettle clients and disrupt sessions.

Changes to room layout, size, availability and accessibility have also raised concerns. These situations can arise when therapy services face growing demand for appointments and staff must share limited facilities for face-to-face, telephone and online sessions.

The space in which therapy takes place really does matter.

Protecting a client’s confidentiality is a foundational principle of psychological therapy.

The ethical principles of acting in the client’s best interests, doing good, avoiding harm and acting fairly may all be compromised if private conversations can be overheard.

Telephone appointments carried out in call-center style settings can increase the good done for a larger number of people by widening access to psychological therapies, particularly in high-volume, low-intensity services—but this must not come at the expense of confidentiality.

Clients are assured that their conversations will remain private but hearing background noises during a call could undermine that assurance. Even if a client is unaware that others are within earshot, therapists still have a duty to protect their confidentiality. If conversations can be overheard, this professional responsibility could be compromised.

There is also the potential for impact on those who inadvertently overhear confidential, sensitive, or distressing information.

In a face-to-face session, hearing footsteps passing along the corridor outside may not be particularly disruptive. But loud noises, conversations outside the door, or interruptions can break the focus of both the therapist and client, affect their relationship, and interfere with the session’s progress.

Room size and accessibility are not just administrative matters. They can also raise ethical concerns.

A cramped consulting room may be inaccessible or uncomfortable for a client or therapist who needs additional space, uses mobility aids, or requires another person to be with them in the room.

Is there enough room for an interpreter, family member, advocate, or even clinical supervisor for the duration of the session if necessary?

The nature of the issues being addressed may influence how comfortable the client may feel sitting close to someone else.

For those who have experienced a trauma or have cultural expectations about maintaining a respectful distance, being forced to sit very close to someone else, even if that person is their therapist, will be hard to accommodate in a small room and may affect their ability to fully engage in the session.

Even seemingly small details can have an impact. For example, are there windows and natural light? Is the space well-ventilated and kept at a comfortable temperature? An enclosed space may be uncomfortable for someone experiencing high levels of anxiety, while poor ventilation could increase the risk of transmitting infection. Small or unsuitable rooms could have a disproportionate and potentially discriminatory effect on clients who are traumatised, have disabilities, are neurodivergent or need additional support.

They may also create barriers for therapists with protected characteristics.

Therapy is not always just two people sitting opposite each other and talking. Depending on the treatment, therapist and client may need to move around, manoeuvre a wheelchair, take pacing breaks, carry out behavioural experiments or exposure exercises, or use techniques such as the empty chair exercise. The space should accommodate the required activities rather than dictate them.

Therapists may also need recording equipment or access to online or written materials.

Furniture matters too: A desk for being able to take notes, different types of seating, a coffee table, or a whiteboard may all play a part in delivering effective therapy.

Although perhaps less common than cramped rooms, a very large space could also present challenges. Unless the extra space is needed for the work being carried out, it may make it harder to create a comfortable, supportive ambiance in a clinical session.

Then there is room availability. Limited access to suitable rooms, or competition to book them at key times, can affect appointment availability and, therefore, clients’ access to therapy and the effective delivery of treatment. The knock-on effect of this is to add to pressures on practitioners and affect their wellbeing.

The space in which therapy is delivered matters, as it can affect the quality and safety of care, equity, client choice, and practitioner well-being.

To meet professional standards of conduct, performance and ethics, therapy services have a responsibility to provide accommodation that supports safe, effective, equitable and sustainable psychological therapies, as well as meeting legal obligations.

Practitioners and service leaders can draw on organisational and professional standards, best practice guidelines and NHS guidance on suitable accommodation when considering how to address or avoid any concerns.

Ensuring workplaces provide suitable spaces can support practitioners’ wellbeing and fitness to practice, reduce the risk of burnout and enhance the service provided to clients.

Helen Macdonald is a BABCP-accredited Cognitive Behavioural Psychotherapist Supervisor and Trainer, a consultant EMDR Therapist, and Senior Clinical Advisor to the BABCP. As a prominent voice within the organisation, she frequently hosts the “Members Matters” podcast.

#4711. Tesla cuts FSD’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit in Europe

Tesla’s driver-assistance system in Europe can no longer be set to drive 50% over the speed limit. The Netherlands’ RDW, which approved the system in April, confirmed today that it signed off on an update capping the speed margin at 10% and officially renaming “FSD Supervised” to Tesla Assisted Driving.

The changes land weeks before EU member states could vote on approving the system across the bloc, and they match the conditions Germany set last month.

The RDW’s notice is the clearest official confirmation of how the system was configured when the Dutch regulator approved FSD Supervised on April 10. The “speed margin,” which lets the system deviate from the detected limit for “safety and traffic flow,” could go up to +50%. On a 100 km/h highway, that’s 150 km/h. In a 30 km/h city zone, it’s 45 km/h.

Now the margin tops out at +10%. It also resets to 0% every time the car starts, and the RDW says other speed-related functions are now disabled by default. It didn’t say which ones.

The new name shows up on the in-car display, in the owner’s manual, and in other driver information on HW4 vehicles. Tesla pushes all of it over the air.

The RDW describes the update as “several minor changes” that Tesla asked it to assess. The regulator says it checked the implementation, found no adverse or unintended effects, and folded the changes into the existing type approval without amending or extending it. It also stresses that the rename doesn’t change what the system does. It’s still driver assistance, and the driver is still responsible.

The RDW notified the nine member states that recognize its approval: Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. That’s 10 countries counting the Netherlands, up from eight at the start of October.

The EU-wide decision still sits with the Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV). The RDW says those talks are confidential and won’t comment on them. As we reported, the EU pushed the vote to December at the earliest, and passing it takes a qualified majority: 15 of 27 member states representing at least 65% of the EU population.

Speed has been the biggest problem for Tesla’s file in Brussels. In June, Sweden asked the EU to reject FSD unless Tesla removed the ability to set speeds above the posted limit. In September, a Brussels pedestrian safety group found the system speeding in 55% of the 30 km/h segments it tested, in a country that had already approved it. France has cited urban speeding as one of its reasons for refusing to recognize the Dutch approval.

Then, on October 6, Germany’s Transport Ministry said it would back EU approval after Tesla agreed to drop the “Full Self-Driving” name, which the ministry called misleading, and to cap speed tolerance at 10%. Today’s RDW update delivers both.

But 10% isn’t what Sweden asked for. Sweden wanted no setting above the limit at all. Several European countries are known for enforcing speed limits strictly.

Good, but that’s only part of the problem. Tesla’s biggest issue with FSD right now is that it doesn’t properly detect the speed limits.

Doing 10% over the limit in North America is almost expected. However, in Europe you can get a speeding ticket for 5 kms over the limit by an automated camera/radar system. When I rent a car over there I drive the posted limit.

Being locked at 10% over the limit doesn’t mean much if you don’t know the actual limit.

The name change is needed globally and it is past due. “Tesla Assisted Driving” describes what the system does. Meanwhile, Tesla still sells the exact same kind of software in the US as “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” for $99 a month. If it’s misleading in Berlin, it’s misleading in California.

Practically, this update gets Tesla Germany’s vote. The question for December is whether a 10% cap is enough for France, Italy, and Spain, or whether Sweden’s zero-tolerance line wins out.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. #4710. Bald eagle mistaken for trashbag on the road to recovery

Published Nov 2, 2026 9:00 AM EST

A Pennsylvania resident recently arrived home to find what looked like an unassuming black trash bag in their yard. But the bag moved and lifted its head. Turns out, it was not a bag, but a bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus). And something was very wrong with her.

A state Game Warden brought the eagle to Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in southern Pennsylvania to be checked out. The bird couldn’t stand and her legs were limp, which is a typical symptom of spinal trauma. Nonetheless, the team also tested the eagle for lead poisoning, and found that she indeed had lead in her system. Even though the eagle wasn’t showing signs of such poisoning, they weren’t surprised by these results.

In a 2022 study published in the journal Science, researchers investigated lead exposure in 1,210 bald and golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos) in North America and found chronic lead poisoning in 46 to 47 percent of both eagles and acute lead poisoning in 27 to 33 percent of bald eagles. Lead exposure in eagles and other avian scavengers mostly occurs when they consume the remains of animals shot with lead ammunition and left behind by hunters.

“Lead poisoning is so common that even eagles brought in for other injuries are now routinely tested for it, and almost all show some level of lead in their system,” Tracie Young, Raven Ridge Wildlife Center director, tells Popular Science.

Even small quantities of lead can be extremely toxic. Lead poisoning can cause brain swelling, trouble breathing, weak muscles, dehydration, starvation, kidney and liver problems, or seizures, Young explains.

“Nerve damage can cause them to lose vision, coordination, and normal movement, so the bird may look ‘drunk’ or not be able to stand,” she continues. “When these eagles are starving, they lose their hunting skills and can’t catch food. As scavengers, they look for roadkill, but because they are uncoordinated, they often get hit by vehicles.”

It’s likely that this is what happened to the trash-bag-looking female eagle in Pennsylvania. At the wildlife center, she received chelation therapy for the lead poisoning. Chelation therapy involves the administration of administering specialized chemical agents that attach to the lead molecules in the bird’s blood and form a compound that is expelled, mostly via urine. The eagle also received physical therapy to regain strength in her legs and mitigate spinal pain and swelling.

Her rehabilitation process has been challenging, but not without its rewards. She is currently able to stand and lives in an outdoor area with an open space where she can continue her rehabilitation process. The eagle is a good candidate for release, but Young says she will require weeks of flight training.

“We urge all hunters and anglers to make a crucial choice: opt for lead-free ammunition and lead-free fishing gear,” the wildlife center wrote in a Facebook post. “This single decision at checkout can significantly improve the lives of countless eagles and other wildlife suffering from lead poisoning.”

#4709. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.

#4708. Volkswagen’s affordable ID. Polo wins German Car of the Year 2027 as EVs dominate

Volkswagen’s new ID. Polo took the overall title of “German Car of the Year 2027,” starting at just €24,995 ($28,000).

After winning in its class among entry-level models (up to €25,000), the VW ID. Polo beat out strong international competition to take the top spot as German Car of the Year for 2027 among all vehicles.

The Volkswagen Group has won two years in a row with a compact EV. Last year, it was the Skoda Elroq.

Volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Polo with the 52 kWh battery at the end of April. In July, it added the entry-level model with the 37 kWh battery, starting at just €24,995 ($28,000) with a WLTP range of up to 207 miles (334 km).

The Life and Style variants are also available with the 37 kWh battery, starting from €29,195 ($32,500).

With DC fast charging speeds of up to 90 kW, the ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 23 minutes.

The prestigious award “confirms what the ID. Polo stands for,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said. He added the entry-level EV “brings electric mobility to where it can make the greatest impact: right into people’s everyday lives.”

Since orders opened at the end of April, Schäfer said “well over 50,000 people have ordered their ID. Polo.”

As the first of what the company calls “a true Volkswagen again,” the ID. Polo is the first to bear an established name and the brand’s new Pure Positive design language.

The jury includes nearly 50 German and international auto journalists, and the award is considered one of the most prestigious in the industry.

The reason this class of vehicles is winning awards is that Europe buys a lot of B-segment vehicles (small hatchbacks) that aren't intended as city-only transport. Many families use them as their only vehicle.

And, up till now, there haven't been many BEVs available in that category.

It is compact, reasonably powerful, reasonably fast charging, acceptable charging rate, has good luggage capacity and feels nice to drive.

In other segments, electric cars swept the awards, with the Kia PV5 van winning in the compact class (€25,000 and €40,000), and Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric taking the top spot in the premium segment (€40,000 to €70,000). Hyundai’s electric sports car, the IONIQ 6 N, won German Performance Car 2027.

Martin Sander, the Group’s sales boss, said earlier this month the company is “seeing a significantly accelerated trend towards all-electric vehicles” in its home market.

VW Group’s Electric Urban Car Family has received nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June. The lineup currently includes the VW ID. Polo and ID. Cross, plus the Cupra Raval and Skoda Epiq, all based on the MEB+ platform.

While those in the US won’t see the entry-level ID. Polo, Volkswagen is set to launch the ID. Tiguan in early 2027 as a replacement for the ID.4.

#4707. A bull and a male donkey’s sexual relationship turns heads

Published Nov 2, 2026 11:00 AM EST

Sex between two animals of the same sex is widespread. Over 1,000 animal species from nematode worms to penguins to cattle all dabble in same-sex interactions. But a relationship between a bull named Achille and a male donkey named Patrocolo is raising eyebrows. The pair lives on a plateau in Ethiopia, and both could have chosen partners of the opposite sex and same species on numerous occasions. However, they continued to choose each other, despite belonging to different owners and only seeing one another when spending time in a pasture. A study published today in the journal Current Biology chronicles this surprising union.

“The sexual interactions between Achille, the bull, and Patroclo, the male donkey, were not isolated events,” Elisabetta Palagi, a study co-author and evolutionary biologist at the Università di Pisa (UNIPI) in Italy, said in a statement. “What really caught our attention was that these interactions were embedded in a very selective and consistent social relationship between the two individuals.”

The team first spotted these interactions while conducting another study earlier this year. They saw Achille mounting Patroclo, and were surprised to see that Patroclo did not try to avoid the bull, kick him, or show any defensive reactions.

“They repeatedly chose to stay close to each other and engaged in many different affiliative behaviors, such as licking, rubbing, and nuzzling, alongside the repeated mounting behavior,” added co-author André da Cruz, a PhD student at UNIPI. “Importantly, this was happening in a social environment where both animals had access to other potential partners, including individuals of both sexes and of their own species.”

The team recorded all of the interactions they witnessed involving either Achille or Patroclo. In total, the observed 51 mountings between the male bull and donkey from March 6 to March 19. In these interactions, Patroclo often presented his hindquarters to Achille and then nipped at the bull. They repeatedly directed most of their sexual and social interactions toward each other, and the team reported no indication from the bull or donkey that either wished to discourage those advances. Achille mounted another male donkey only twice, and that other male showed avoidance behaviors and threatening expressions, like flattened ears.

“We believe the key finding is not simply that a bull mounted a male donkey,” said study co-author Martina Francesconi, also a PhD student at UNIPI. “It is that this unusual sexual behavior was part of a broader, selective social relationship. Our observations suggest that it cannot be easily explained simply by a lack of alternative mating opportunities, although we cannot say from this study exactly what function these sexual interactions may have had.”

According to the team, these observations have wider implications for our understanding of how sexual behavior is a complex social trait that goes beyond its role in reproduction. It also raises important questions for future studies, including if these interactions are primarily related to social bonding, what the benefits are, and if they play a role in reducing tension or maintaining relationships. In previous studies, same-sex mounting in nonhuman primates appears to be a form of conflict resolution and way to strengthen bonds, and may help male macaques reproduce more successfully.

“More broadly, we would like to better understand how social relationships shape sexual behavior and how behavioral flexibility allows animals to navigate complex social environments,” said Palagi. “We see this study as a starting point for asking these broader questions.”

#4706. When Grief Changes a Family, Does Distance Mean Love Is Lost?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

When a family member dies, we may imagine the surviving family members leaning on one another, sharing memories, and finding comfort in their common loss. This doesn’t always happen, as grief doesn't always bring families closer. In some cases, it creates more distance between the people who might understand our loss best.

In Hallmark's "A Season of Promises," sisters Heidi and Sophie have grown apart following their mother's death four years ago. We see their obvious differences while we watch a home video from 30 years ago. Viewers may expect the sisters to have their issues, but we soon learn that they no longer interact after the death of their mother. They reach out to one another only after their father, Ed, experiences a health scare. After realizing how alone he is, they decide to help him find love again while also encouraging him to seek out grief support.

While the movie follows their matchmaking efforts, its more interesting story is about what happens to family relationships after a significant loss. It portrays three family members who experienced the same loss and who are grieving in three very different ways.

The death of a family member doesn't simply remove one person from a family. Instead, it changes the relationships among everyone who remains. Family systems theory suggests that families are interconnected systems. When something happens to one member, the effects ripple throughout the family. The loss of a parent, for example, may change how siblings interact, how responsibilities are distributed, and how family members understand their new roles. Family members grieve not only the person who moved on but also the role they no longer occupy.

The Double ABC-X model of family stress can also help explain why some families struggle following a loss. Families must manage not only the original stressful event but also the additional demands that accumulate afterward. Their ability to adapt depends partly on available resources and how family members interpret their circumstances. Sometimes, the difficulty isn't that family members don't care about one another. It's that they don't know how to support one another when their needs are different.

For many people, sibling relationships are the longest-lasting relationships in their lives. Siblings often know us before our friendships, romantic partnerships, and professional identities develop. They share family histories, childhood experiences, and memories that no one else can fully replicate, but the length of a relationship does not mean its closeness will remain constant.

Sibling relationships often move through periods of connection and disengagement. Geographic distance, different life circumstances, competing responsibilities, and unresolved disagreements can all influence how frequently siblings interact. Heidi and Sophie are examples. Although their relationship has become strained, the distance isn’t permanent, as their concern for their father brings them together again. Sophie’s love interest made a particularly meaningful observation, after listening to her discuss her complicated sibling relationship: "Families are messy. It doesn't mean you stop loving each other."

I appreciated Hallmark including this interaction because so many of us feel like having messy families signals trouble, but it’s a reality of having complex and interdependent relationships that can be impacted by stressors. Sophie's and Heidi’s relationship captures the reality of relationships. They also demonstrate the notion that love and closeness are not necessarily the same thing. We can love family members deeply while needing distance from them. We can disagree about the past without erasing the relationships that shaped us. Disengagement is not always a sign that a relationship has failed. Sometimes it reflects a period when family members need space to manage their own lives, emotions, or identities.

The Circumplex Model of Marital and Family Systems identifies two important dimensions of family functioning: cohesion and flexibility. Cohesion describes the emotional bonds among family members. Flexibility refers to a family's ability to adjust its roles, relationships, and expectations when circumstances change.

Healthy family relationships generally require a balance of both. Too little cohesion (i.e., disengagement) may leave family members feeling disconnected, while too much cohesion (e.g., enmeshment) may make it difficult for individuals to develop independence or establish boundaries.

Similarly, families that struggle to adapt may find themselves expecting relationships to remain exactly as they were, even after significant life changes. For Heidi and Sophie, rebuilding their relationship doesn't necessarily mean returning to the closeness they experienced before their mother's death. Instead, it may require recognizing that they have changed and allowing their relationship to change with them.

Connection leaves room for individuality. Family members do not have to experience grief identically, make the same decisions, or maintain constant contact to remain important to one another.

Perhaps one of the movie's most insightful moments occurs when one of the daughters confides in a new love interest that she wants to fix her father's grief. He gently suggests that perhaps her father doesn't need someone to fix his grief and that maybe he needs someone willing to sit in it with him. This distinction is important.

When someone we love is hurting, our instinct is often to make the pain disappear. We offer solutions, encourage new activities, or try to help them move forward. These efforts usually come from a place of love, but they may also reflect our own discomfort with watching someone suffer. Grief, however, is not a problem that another person can solve.

Social support can help people cope with loss, but support doesn't always require action. Sometimes it means listening without offering advice, acknowledging difficult emotions, or simply being present. The sisters' efforts to find their father a romantic partner reflect their desire to see him happy again, but his grief cannot necessarily be resolved by introducing someone new into his life. A new relationship may bring joy, but it doesn't erase the significance of the relationship that was lost.

Hallmark movies typically offer satisfying resolutions, and A Season of Promises is no exception. The movie raises a question that extends beyond its Christmas setting: What does it mean to remain a family when our relationships no longer look the way they did? Families experience periods of closeness, conflict, loss, and disengagement. Not every disagreement can be resolved immediately, and not every relationship will return to its previous form.

Maintaining family relationships can mean accepting that people grieve differently, need different amounts of connection, or require time apart. What matters is whether family members can make room for one another's needs while being honest about their own. Perhaps the lesson of A Season of Promises isn't that families must always come back together. Instead, it’s that relationships can change without losing their significance.

Hallmark says: A loved one's health scare can be the catalyst to bring a family back together, along with the help of Christmas magic.

Psychology says: Family relationships don't have to remain consistently close to be meaningful. Healthy families make room for different experiences of grief, changing relationships, and the understanding that supporting someone doesn't always mean fixing their pain.

The verdict: Hallmark captures the complexity of grief and how differently it can be experienced within the same family. The movie portrays a family struggling with loss, the ways grief can strain relationships, and the challenges of grieving both individually and together. Ultimately, the family comes to recognize that moving forward doesn't mean returning to how things were before their loss. Instead, they learn to embrace a new normal, one that makes room for grief, changing relationships, and continued love.

#4704. Aloe found in ancient Egyptian mummy skull

Published Nov 2, 2026 12:58 PM EST

Archaeologists have identified a previously undocumented ingredient used in ancient Egyptian mummifications—and a famous medieval medicine concocted from the mummies themselves. At Germany’s Marburg University, researchers pinpointed traces of aloe-associated plant material in a 2,700-year-old mummy skull, and a popular centuries’ old apothecary cure-all known as Mumia vera aegyptiaca.

There is no one way to make a mummy. Mummification methods have varied across the world for thousands of years, even within a single culture. Ancient Egyptians honed their own processes over generations, and archaeologists are still sifting through millennia’s worth of artifacts and texts to better understand the iconic postmortem procedures.

Egyptology first truly took off in Europe during the late 18th century, but people’s fascination with mummies goes much further back in time. However, the long and complex medicinal history of mummy-derived treatments collectively called Mumia likely began as a 12th century mistranslation. Persian pharmacists often used a black pitch called mumiya in wound care, which medieval translators of Latin later mistook for similarly dark materials used in Egyptian mummification. This eventually led to an entire trade network centered on the import of powdered mummy remains sold by apothecaries as a Mumia cure-all—and sometimes even an aphrodisiac—for centuries.

Archaeologists have already documented many mummification ingredients derived from various minerals, animals, and plants. These span a range of coniferous tars and reins, oils, fats, beeswax, and bitumen, as well as rarer regional plant distillations like dammar and elemi. Knowing there is still much more to learn, the team at Marburg University recently analyzed 24 historically related objects stored at various institutions. These included an Egyptian mummified skull dated to the 8th century BCE, as well as an 18th century historical preparation of Mumia housed at Heidelberg Pharmacy Museum.

Their findings were recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and offer the first molecular evidence of mummy-related materials directly derived from aloe. This is particularly important, since “aloe” often historically referred to a variety of plants like agarwood outside the Aloe genus. According to Tanja Pommerening, a study co-author and director of Marburg University’s Institute for the History of Pharmacy and Medicine, the detection of aloe in Mumia is also particularly significant. Prior to this study, many researchers assumed medieval authors drew their Mumia recipes from biblical passages. These include John 19:39, which references a “mixture of myrrh and aloes.”

“The new findings suggest that this association may have deeper historical roots,” explained Pommerening.

However, since only two of the 24 artifacts in the study yielded traces of aloe, the frequency of the plant’s use in mummification and Mumia remains unclear. It’s possible that preparers may have only incorporated the material during certain historical periods, or depending on its availability. Still, Pommerening and her colleagues plan to continue similar examinations of other historical objects.

“Our goal is not only to analyze the chemical composition of ancient medicines and embalming materials, but also to gain a deeper understanding of their production, use, historical transmission, and cultural context,” added study co-author and Marburg University biologist Raphael Reher.

Hospital ratings have become an important resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

The annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

New research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

Around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

#4701. How to Live a Life You Would Never Have Chosen

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 10, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Twenty years ago, I was diagnosed with a form of autoimmune arthritis. I’d had symptoms since college, but I had never been properly diagnosed. Two of my three brothers suffer from a form of the same disease. By the time of my diagnosis, it had seeped into every aspect of my life.

Up until then I was able to make accommodations through rest, early bedtimes, and appropriate exercise. However, in my early 40s, things heated up to the point that it became difficult to work. I have now been home and disabled for 13 years. On a good day, I may feel normal for a few hours in the afternoon. But if I overdo the most banal of activity, I will pay with more fatigue and joint pain later.

This is all to say that not feeling well and all the medical complications this entails are now the main subject of my life. As a psychiatrist who was in practice for 23 years, I am very familiar with people who are in a similar boat. Most of my patients did not feel well due to mental suffering (although some physical symptoms, such as fatigue, weakness, headache, and GI upset were common).

One thing all of us had in common was that the rest of the world had little awareness of our plight. In normal life, your body strikes a simple deal: give it ample rest and nutrition, and it allows you to go through your day and attend to what needs to be done without making a fuss. Other than meal and bedtime, it doesn’t bother you with demands for attention. When you are chronically ill, this is turned on its head. Your body demands attention like a fractious child. Due to its various aches and pains, it requires constant adjustments in your activity and mindset. Trying to feel better and dealing with how you feel is your full-time job.

Assuming, as is sadly the case, that many of these illnesses never get better, the question arises of how to live your life in the face of constant discomfort and a background of an increasing number of losses and limitations. For those of us in that situation, this is the real task of our days. The temptation and natural response is to try to feel better and imagine a better day just around the corner. But this makes you a hamster on a wheel.

What then is the path? Surely, we cannot give up some hope of improvement and attempts to stay healthy and, just perhaps, find a way forward. No, don’t give this up. Keep it on the back burner. But there is more work to be done.

The two central tasks of chronic illness are acceptance and a way to find meaning in a life you would never have chosen.

But don’t acceptance and hope contradict one another? How can we accept our losses, limitations and feeling poorly each day while we work and hope to improve our lot? The way to accomplish this is to remain aware that you are treading two paths. Yes, you must go to the doctor. Do your exercises and get a great deal of rest. You must avoid taxing situations and stay home a great deal of the time. Here, in fact, is where acceptance begins. It is exactly in living your life in ways that you would not choose where you seek to open yourself and accept your situation without a mental struggle. Letting go of this struggle does not mean letting go of hope for some change.

Acceptance includes a frank and often painful acknowledgment of where you are and what is lost to you. But in the long run, the pain of reliving your losses over and over is alleviated by acceptance. You must do your best to remain as healthy as possible while simultaneously acknowledging your limitations.

Part of this is a mourning process no different than the loss of a loved one. There is anger, bargaining, sadness, and hopefully acceptance. No more struggling with what might have been. This is harder for the chronically sick as the losses continue and some of these feelings will be revisited. That is part of the work.

When I first stopped working, I wondered how much more of myself could I lose and still feel like me. It turns out that I can lose a great deal and still be me. I have always understood myself as the sum of what I’ve accomplished in even one day. That obviously no longer works. You come to realize that despite your losses you remain yourself in the most fundamental of ways. How you treat people, what you value, and where you spend your limited attention continue to define you.

What I have found to be a more difficult question is finding meaning in your new existence. This is unfortunately an exercise that is not based on an equal distribution of luck in life. Those with more resources, more connections, and just plainly more opportunities have more chances of finding how to live a meaningful life. Here, as with anything else, you must play the cards you are dealt.

Meaning is based on values and will develop from what we find important. Interest and the involvement of other people are good places to start. But if you are stuck at home and cannot reliably get out to meetings, especially in the evening, how is this done? Unfortunately, there is no formula. Use of the Internet is a modern godsend to people like us. It makes possible connections to groups and causes that would otherwise be inaccessible. In addition, there are ways to learn new things, new skills, hobbies, etc.

There are times when this has felt to me like make-work. Usually, I have reverted to writing about psychiatry and illness, the two things I know and care about. But people vary a great deal in these personal matters. You do not need to start a charity, write a book, or learn a foreign language. Creativity, connecting to others, or just learning something new may bring new meaning to your days.

As I write this, though, it feels unsatisfactory. Recommending hobbies on YouTube does not truly feel like a way to find meaning, but rather more of a pastime. The very best suggestions I have given are not meaningful in and of themselves. Rather, they are pathways into your own deeper sense of importance and interest. This becomes a highly personal matter that only you can judge.

However personal and unique to you, it is an important part of your path through life with chronic illness. The journey is no longer through the outside world—as illness takes much of that away—but into yourself. The various pastimes are doorways into your internal life. This is where you now spend most of your time and where you must plant a flag to declare the continued importance of your very existence.

#4700. Dinosaur blood found in fossils for the first time

Published Nov 2, 2026 3:00 PM EST

Paleontologists regularly discover fossilized dinosaur bones, but they sometimes locate footprints and prehistoric shells. On rare occasions, researchers have even identified the ancient indentations of a dinosaur’s skin or feathers. But fossilized cells? Researchers have long assumed such microscopic levels of preservation were impossible. But, once again, nature has proven otherwise.

In a study published today in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), an international team of paleontologists confirmed the presence of intact biomolecules and mineralized red blood cells inside fossils of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur. Although previous work has suggested similar possibilities, the team’s research is the first to chemically identify oxygen-carrying blood compounds known as heme.

“This really is a landmark discovery,” Kliti Grice, a study co-author and chemist at Curtin University in Australia, said in a statement. “These findings challenge longstanding assumptions that certain biomolecules such as hemoglobin cannot survive deep time.”

The evidence exists inside the fossilized limb bones of a juvenile Aratasaurus museunacionali. Discovered in 2008, A. museunacionali was an Early Cretaceous theropod that lived in present-day northeastern Brazil. The fossils suggest a dinosaur measuring over 10 feet long and weighing about 75 pounds, but given its young age, A. museunacionali likely grew even larger.

After carefully examining thin slices of the fossils, paleontologists located the mineralized red blood cell molecular components, along with a complex manganese oxide called hausmannite. This material helped maintain the cellular structures of heme, a ring-shaped molecule that contains iron and binds many proteins, especially hemoglobin. The hausmannite also helped preserve additional biomolecules found in the blood, such as the amino acids in collagen. The study’s authors theorize this level of preservation could only occur following a rapid burial in an environment that was rich in microbes, but low in oxygen at the same time.

Grice and her collaborators said that their discovery has wider implications for molecular-level paleontology. Further study could help advance our understanding of blood’s evolution, dinosaur metabolism, and ancient animals’ activity levels. The knowledge that this type of preservation is possible at all could even extend far beyond Earth. If such delicate biomolecules fossilize over millions of years in harsh environments, then it’s possible similar traces of life may linger elsewhere in the universe.

#4699. Pennsylvania is way ahead on NEVI charging – now comes another $37M

Pennsylvania is putting $37 million in federal NEVI funding toward what PennDOT says will be 515 new public EV charging ports across the Philadelphia region, including curbside chargers.

The awards cover Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, and Philadelphia counties. PennDOT says the projects will expand public charging availability by 27% across the region and 53% in Philadelphia.

For drivers without a driveway, curbside charging gives them somewhere to plug in while parked near home.

It’s Electric PA received $2.93 million for 157 on-street Level 2 ports across 13 Philadelphia neighborhoods. Voltpost received funding for another 62 curbside ports across the four suburban counties.

Fast charging is getting funding, too. PositivEnergy received $7.2 million for 54 DC fast-charging ports at 11 Philadelphia Parking Authority lots. Tesla received two $392,000 awards for eight ports each at Royal Farms in Broomall and Wawa in Plymouth Meeting.

The money comes from the federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program, created by the Biden administration’s Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. Pennsylvania’s five-year allocation is $171.5 million.

NEVI initially focused on fast charging along designated highway corridors. States can spend the money more broadly after the Federal Highway Administration certifies that their corridor charging requirements have been met. Pennsylvania received that certification on September 22, 2025.

In fact, Pennsylvania has built 54 EV charging stations using NEVI funds so far – more than double the number of any other state.

PennDOT’s community charging program supports both Level 2 and DC fast charging. Its published program minimum requirements include at least four ports per proposed station, at least 6 kW per port, two ADA-compliant parking spaces, and J1772 or CCS connectors on every port. Equipment must also meet Buy America requirements.

PennDOT lists 71 awards in this southeastern round as part of its roughly $100 million statewide community charging effort.

Applications for the western region close November 20. Central and eastern Pennsylvania applications close March 12, 2027.

#4698. Watchful mama bear Gemini wins 2026 Helicopter Mom Award

Published Nov 2, 2026 4:07 PM EST

Even bears can be helicopter parents. The term coined in the 1990s by child development researchers Foster Cline and Jim Fay describes overly cautious parents who constantly monitor, control, and hover over (like a helicopter) their children’s activities out of fear.

For these watchful tendencies, the U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska has awarded a brown bear (Ursus arctos) named Gemini with the 2026 Helicopter Mom Award.

“We understand her choice, weighing the dangers of being around other bears at a prime fishing location,” the rangers write. “Still, we hope we see a lot more of them next year.”

The numbers also back up Gemini and other mother bears’ watchfulness. Brown bear cubs in Alaska have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent depending on the location. Gemini has also had cubs in 2023 and 2024.

The Rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The vast area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Like their beefy counterparts further north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here exhibits their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.
