#4636. Losing Weight in Your 50s May Protect Your Heart Health Later in Life

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to new research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, said Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

“By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she said.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz said the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

She said researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”

Weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he said. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

“It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy said.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy said. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham said the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

The study showed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also said the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham said adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive plan,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

#4635. Toyota updates the 2027 RAV4 PHEV with an NACS port and up to 52 miles of EV range

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 is bringing a few major updates, including an added NACS charge port on all plug-in hybrid (PHEV) models.

The RAV4 was Toyota’s best-selling nameplate in the US last year and consistently ranks among America’s most popular vehicles alongside the Ford F-Series and Chevrolet Silverado.

For the 2027 model year, Toyota added several notable upgrades. The 2027 Toyota RAV4 will be available with hybrid (HEV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with available front- or all-wheel drive (AWD).

The biggest change is that all 2027 RAV4 PHEV models now have a built-in NACS charge port with Level 3 DC fast-charging capabilities.

The NACS port is on the driver’s side and lets drivers use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. All PHEV grades also include an 11 kW onboard AC charger.

Powered by Toyota’s sixth-generation PHEV system, the plug-in RAV4 has standard AWD with a combined output of 321 horsepower. The setup includes a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, two electric motors, and a high-capacity traction battery.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 PHEV offers up to 52 miles of pure electric range on the base SE trim. It will be available in four trims: SE, XSE, Woodland, and GR Sport.

Toyota updated the suspension system in the Woodland grade for the 2027 model year with new springs, shocks, and jounce bumpers, giving it 9.1″ of ground clearance.

The Woodland trim adds a rugged look with standard All-Terrain tires, Roof Rails with Cross Bars, and a Tow Hitch Receiver. It also features new all-weather floor and cargo mats.

Lastly, the RAV4 GR Sport trim is for those who want a more performance-oriented, sporty style, with GT-tuned suspension and steering, sports seating, and a standard PHEV powertrain with AWD.

Inside, the 2027 RAV4 includes a standard 12.3″ digital cluster and a 10.5″ touchscreen with the Toyota Audio Multimedia system, plus wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

A 12.9″ touchscreen with a JBL Premium Audio system with 9 speakers is standard on the Limited trim and available on the XSE grade.

All 2027 Toyota RAV4s come with standard Toyota Safety Sense 4.0, which includes safety and convenience features such as Lane Departure Alert with Steering Assist, Full-Speed Range Dynamic Radar Cruise Control, Proactive Driving Assist, and a Pre-Collision System with Pedestrian Detection.

They don't make it easy to find out just what that level 3 charging rate is or how big the battery is. If it's as slow as an old Bolt, could take as long as 20 minutes to charge. If the DC charge hardware is more modern, could be 5-10. Would still be a weird choice, but if you need to stop for a drink of a bathroom anyway, why not?

2027 Toyota RAV4 HEV models are expected to begin arriving at dealerships later this year, while the PHEV models are expected to follow in early 2027.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 HEV starts at $32,300 (LE FWD), and the PHEV version starts at $42,100, not including the $1,595 destination fee.

With the 2027 models on the way, the best deals are on the current 2026 RAV4 PHEV. Want to see what’s available near you? You can use our link to find Toyota RAV4 plug-in hybrids near you, along with any local offers.

#4634. The best solar generators for 2026, tested and reviewed

Updated Nov 5, 2026 10:37 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

Solar generators can make your life a little easier on a good day or save you on a bad day. These powerful power packs offer huge battery capacity that can fuel large devices and even appliances in a pinch. They’re great in an emergency, but they’re also essential tailgating and camping equipment. We chose the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 as our best overall pick, but there are plenty of options to fit your specific neeeds.

As an avid outdoorsman, I’ve had the opportunity to test a wide range of outdoor gear, including mobile and off-grid electrification equipment like solar-powered generators, as well as inverter and dual-fuel generators. These became particularly essential when the pandemic forced my travels to become domestic rather than international, which prompted me to outfit a van for long-term road-tripping.

To bring my work along for the ride, I needed a constant portable power source to charge my laptop, a portable fridge, lighting, and a myriad of devices and tools … even electric bikes. As a result, I’ve tried all the leading portable power stations (and plenty that aren’t leading, too), so I know precisely what separates the best from the blah. I’ve written all about it (and other outdoor tech) for publications, including the Daily Beast, Thrillist, the Manual, Popular Science, and more. There were cases when my own opinion resulted in a tie, so I looked to reviews from actual customers to determine which solar generators delivered the most satisfaction to the most users. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, Explorer 1000 v2 and Explorer 300 v2 joined the list in November 2026 based on their published specs and how they stack up against the units we’ve tested; we haven’t put any of them through our own testing yet.

If you’re thinking about dropping big money on a solar generator, consider shopping on big shopping holidays like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday. These are expensive devices, and they experience their largest discounts around those times. That said, they frequently sell below list price, even when it’s not a retail holiday, so click through to find out.

The solar generators on this list span a wide range of budgets, from a few hundred dollars to a few thousand. They cover several uses, from camping to backup for your home. Only you know all the factors that make one of these the best solar generator for you, but we think that one of these will get the job done.

Why it made the cut: No other solar generator delivers such an excellent balance of portability, capacity, and performance.

There are a lot of excellent solar generators on this list, many of which are competitive rivals for the top spot, but none offer such an excellent fusion of capacity, portability, and well-considered design as the Bluetti Elite 200 V2. With a capacity of 2,073 watt-hours, it hits the sweet spot that will deliver on the needs of the vast majority of users.

At the same time, its compact dimensions make it easy to fit almost anywhere, though at 53.4 pounds it’s a two-hand lift. That makes it an easy pick for packing in a trunk while heading outdoors, storing in a closet for backup power, or simply having around for a convenient, mobile power source.

It also offers high output for its size. Its 2,600W running output was already hefty enough, and Bluetti’s Power Lifting mode can run resistive loads such as kettles and hair dryers at up to 3,900W. Its 1000W solar input capacity equips it for a large solar panel array, and its 1,800W wall input capacity will charge it from zero to full in about 1.4 hours, according to Bluetti.

While power station apps are notoriously glitchy, the Bluetti app is user-friendly and allows for remote monitoring and adjustment. Most users will find it has plenty of ports, including four AC ports, USB-A and USB-C ports, and a 120W car port, though there is no 30A or 50A RV plug.

I’ve found that its squared-off design is ideal for fitting into a tight storage space or building into a small van conversion. The LiFePO4 battery has a lifespan of over 6,000 cycles, and the whole unit feels plenty durable. Indeed, I have knocked my test unit around more than a little. It seems no worse for wear.

For most mid-sized portable power purposes, the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 does pretty much everything right.

Why it made the cut: The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 keeps the 2kWh capacity that made the old Explorer 2000 Plus our former top pick and drops about 20 pounds doing it.

At 39.5 pounds, the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 is a 2,042Wh LiFePO4 station one person can lift into a hatchback without planning the move. Jackery rates it for 2,200W of continuous output and 4,400W surge, enough for a full-size fridge, a microwave or most corded tools. It refills from a wall outlet in about 1.7 hours, and Jackery says it keeps about 95 percent of its charge after 12 months in storage, so it can sit in a closet between outages.

The weight savings cost you the 2000 Plus’s expansion option. Jackery says the v2 doesn’t take expansion batteries, so 2,042Wh is what you get. If you need room to grow, the EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus below is the better fit.

Why it made the cut: The EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus itself is high-capacity, high-output, and exceptionally well-designed, and can expand up to 11kWh.

The EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus is a solid contender for “best overall,” and the only reason it didn’t get it is because it’s more of a power station than most people need. But if you do need more power station, it delivers.

The standalone unit’s 3,072Wh capacity is plenty for powering an RV or van conversion, an off-grid worksite, or a home during a blackout. Its 3,600W output can run most household devices and larger appliances, EcoFlow’s X-Boost mode lets it run some higher-wattage resistive appliances at reduced voltage, and its 7,200W surge capacity handles the spike when an air conditioner, appliance, or power tool switches on. It has six charging options, and a wall outlet alone gets it to 80 percent in about 89 minutes if you’re readying for a storm or trip. Storm Guard Mode will monitor the weather and charge the unit automatically if severe weather is coming.

All that’s great, but what I really like about it is how much consideration went into various design elements. For example, whoever thought of having the rear port doors slide into protective slots is a genius. It’s a heavy unit, but the sturdy handle and telescoping wheels make it easy to move around. It’s equipped with a 30A outlet so it can plug directly into an RV, and a good number of other ports.

Excellent all around. If you need a larger, potentially expandable solar generator that offers a good dose of portability, it’s hard to beat.

Why it made the cut: The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 covers a weekend of car-camping loads at about 24 pounds, small enough to ride on the floor behind the front seat.

Car camping runs on small, steady loads: a 12V cooler, phone and headlamp charging, maybe a string of lights. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 has 1,070Wh of LiFePO4 battery for that, and Jackery rates the cells for 4,000 cycles before they drop to 70 percent capacity. Its 1,500W inverter (3,000W surge) also handles an electric kettle at the campsite.

Two of Jackery’s 200W SolarSaga panels plug straight into its two DC ports, which is the full 400 watts it accepts. Jackery quotes about 7.5 hours to refill it from a single 200W panel, so plan on most of a sunny day if you bring just one.

Why it made the cut: Huge expandability, excellent performance, and unsurpassed solar capability make the Bluetti Apex 300 a must for reliable off-grid power.

Bluetti’s Apex 300 does everything you can find in the best off-grid solar generators, then takes it a step further. It has huge storage capacity that gets bigger and bigger depending on your needs (and budget, since all those batteries certainly aren’t cheap). You can scale up its output wattage to handle pretty much anything you throw at it. While it’s definitely very heavy, once you’ve got it in place, it’s also very intuitive to operate. Amazon sells it bundled with Bluetti’s B300K expansion battery, which doubles the standalone 2,764.8Wh capacity to 5,529.6Wh.

But where the Apex 300 truly excels is in its solar input capacity. Its standard dual 1,200W solar input is already great in its own right, but when you add on the SolarX 4K, it adds up to 4,000W more. Bluetti says a system of three Apex 300 units, each with a SolarX 4K, takes up to 19,200W of solar, enough for a serious off-grid array.

Why it made the cut: Great specs and portability, plus Jackery’s ZeroDrain reliability, make the HomePower 3000 a safe bet for outages.

From my experience, the most important thing you need from a solar generator for home backup is reliability. I’ve been disappointed more than once to find that my power station hasn’t held its charge while in storage. To that end, the Jackery HomePower 3000, equipped with its ZeroDrain tech, which Jackery says helps it hold a charge in storage, is ready when you need it. The HomePower series is a new divergence from Jackery’s already popular Explorer series, and it moves the brand forward in terms of offering not only the aforementioned ZeroDrain, but more capacity and performance for its size.

Slightly smaller and lighter than Jackery’s older Explorer 2000 Plus, it nevertheless has 1,000Wh more capacity, and it’s significantly smaller than the 3000 Pro while delivering comparable capacity and performance. That, combined with its ZeroDrain shelf life, makes it ideal for keeping in a dry closet or garage until the next outage.

Why it made the cut: Its sodium-ion battery lets the Bluetti Pioneer Na charge at 5°F, well below the point where most lithium-based power stations stop accepting a charge.

Bluetti has been making some of the best lithium-based power stations out there, and now it sells what it bills as the first commercially available sodium-ion portable power station. Typically, power stations operate poorly in cold temperatures, and store in the cold even worse. The Pioneer Na, however, can charge at temperatures as low as 5°F and discharge as low as -13°F, according to Bluetti. Most lithium-based stations can still discharge below freezing, but they usually can’t charge there, which is the bigger problem on a cold trip.

At the same time, the performance is good. While the 900Wh capacity isn’t massive, it’s plenty for smaller-scale uses like camping or short-term backup power during an outage. And the 1,500W output is more than enough to power a fridge, TV, and a handful of devices at once. I’m also a big fan of its zippy charging, as Bluetti says it reaches 80 percent in 35 minutes, and full in 52, with 1,900 watts of combined wall and solar input. For weathering the cold, it’s the one to get.

Why it made the cut: The Jackery Explorer 300 v2 keeps the original’s small footprint but moves to a LiFePO4 battery that Jackery rates for 4,000 cycles.

Though it isn’t quite as impressive as our top picks for best overall and best high-capacity, the Jackery Explorer 300 v2 is compact, light, and a decent amount of power for its price. Less a mobile power station than an upscale power bank, the 8.16-pound Explorer 300 v2 handles device charging when you’re camping, on a job site, driving, or just need some power away from an outlet. Its 288Wh capacity isn’t huge, but it’s enough to keep phones, cameras and a laptop topped off, or run a small fan or light for a few hours. The 300W inverter (600W surge) won’t run a coffee maker, but it has a 100W USB-C port, and Jackery says a wall outlet refills it in about 76 minutes.

We tested the original Explorer 300, the portable power station this one replaces, for several months, and it came in handy numerous times, especially during the winter when power outages abound. At one point, we had it powering two phones, a MacBook, and a small light. We haven’t tested the v2 yet, but it’s in the same size class with a longer-lived battery: Jackery rates its LiFePO4 cells for 4,000 cycles before they drop to 70 percent of their original capacity.

Our original review unit got banged around in car trunks, duffel bags, and other less-than-luxurious accommodations with no issues. If you catch one of these on sale, get it and stick it in a cabinet. You’ll be extremely glad to have it around when the need arises.

Over the past few years, solar generators have exploded onto the market. There are now dozens of different brands that largely look more or less the same at a glance. The fact is, there are only a few standouts among a sea of knockoffs. Here’s what to look for to ensure you’re getting a great one:

A portable solar generator comes in a wide range of sizes, but a generator’s size doesn’t automatically make it capable of storing a lot of power. In fact, most are disappointingly limited and unable to store much more juice than a portable charger.

To properly check a generator’s storage, you must look at its capacity, measured in watt-hours (Wh). One watt-hour is the equivalent of 1 watt flowing over the course of an hour. The best solar generators offer capacities of several hundred and sometimes several thousand watt-hours. That doesn’t mean, however, that it will provide power for several hundred or several thousand hours. Any generator will ultimately last a different amount of time, depending on what’s plugged into it.

It’s easy to predict how long a generator will last when you use it to power one thing. For example, if you were to power a 100-watt bulb using a power station with a capacity of 500 watt-hours, it would stay lit for five continuous hours. Add a portable fridge with a 50W average draw, a phone charger drawing up to 18W, a 3W mini-fan, and runtime drops accordingly. The more capacity, the better.

No solar generator will hold a charge forever, so you want one capable of charging as quickly and easily as possible. This is where we put the “renewable” into “renewable energy.”

All of the power stations included in this roundup can be charged by connecting them to solar panels (hence the designation “solar generators”). Still, you also want to look for the ability to charge via other sources like wall outlets and your vehicle’s 12-volt plug. This ensures that you can charge up whether you’re off-grid in the sun, plugged in while preparing at home, or using your dash socket on the go.

You must also monitor a model’s charging input capacity, measured in watts (W). For example, a solar-powered generator with a max input of 100W can take in a continuous flow of up to 100 watts, which is about the minimum that you’ll reasonably want to look for. Most of the generators below have input capacities of at least a few hundred watts when charging via solar, so a few 50- to 200-watt solar panels will max them out.

Solar generators need to keep the power coming in and going out. The best solar generators can simultaneously charge all your intended devices via whatever plugs are necessary.

Any portable power station worth your money will have a high output capacity so you can charge many devices, even if they require a lot of juice. At a minimum, you’ll want a generator that can put out 300 watts at a time, though you’ll want at least 500 for larger tasks.

The best solar generators should also offer a variety of output plugs, including AC outlets, USB-A, USB-C, and even 12-volt DC outlets like the one in your vehicle dash. This ensures you can charge several devices simultaneously regardless of their plug. The number of ports you’ll need will vary depending on how many devices you need to power, but it should have at least a couple of AC outlets and enough USB-C and USB-A ports, at suitable wattages, for your devices.

While portable battery sources have been around for a while now, over the past several decades, they’ve been pretty heavy, unwieldy things. One of the most exciting aspects of the latest generation of solar generators is that they’ve become much more physically compact.

Suppose you plan on taking a generator camping or working it into a van conversion where every square inch matters; well, size and weight become major considerations. All of the products we’ve recommended are about the size of one or two shoeboxes, three at the most. The lightest weighs about 7 pounds, while the heaviest standalone unit is about 84 pounds. Most fall somewhere between 30 and 60 pounds.

If you’re using your generator as a more or less stationary source of backup power at home, portability isn’t a huge issue. Still, we generally recommend keeping weight and size in mind; you never know when you’ll need it for something other than a backup. (Plus, who wants to lug around something heavy and awkward if they don’t have to?)

Another consideration regarding portability involves the necessity for accessories, which can impact how easy it is to move and use your generator. Some generators, for example, require a lot of removable battery packs, which can be a hassle when you’re on the go or packing a vehicle. All of the picks on our list work on their own, though solar charging requires compatible panels and cables.

As with any product you expect to last, durability and all-around quality craftsmanship are essential. This is especially true if you plan on lugging your generator around on camping and road trips. Many subpar power stations are made from cheap components and flimsy plastic that doesn’t feel like it will hold up under the rigors of the road.

Durability isn’t something you can determine by reading a spec sheet off the internet. You’ve actually got to take the generator out, use it a bunch, and see how it holds up. I’ve verified the durability of these recommendations via a combination of my own actual field tests and reviews culled from countless real product owners. The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, Explorer 1000 v2 and Explorer 300 v2 are the exceptions; we haven’t tested them yet.

It’s easy to underestimate how much capacity you need. 1,000 watt-hours might sound like a lot, but if you’re going to power a converted van with a portable fridge, lights, and occasional phone and laptop top-off, that 1,000 watt-hours will go faster than you expect. I used a setup like this and know from personal experience that you should always overestimate how much power you’ll need.A generator with a capacity under 1,000Wh can keep electronics charged. A larger one with 1,000 to 1,500Wh should be the minimum for road trips where you’ll need it to last multiple days between full charges. For a house or worksite where you expect to use some serious energy, like a full-sized refrigerator or power tools, you’re going to want to start looking at the biggest possible power stations that can be daisy-chained to external batteries.If you want to get precise, there is an equation:1. Estimate how many hours you’ll need to power various devices. For example, if you want to power two light bulbs for two hours, you need two hours of operation.2. Add up the total wattage necessary: the two bulbs are 60 watts each, so you need 120 watts.3. Multiply these together to find the total watt-hours needed: 2 x 120 = 240Wh. Leave room for conversion losses and a reserve, and you’d want at least a 300Wh solar generator. That might sound like a lot for two lightbulbs, but remember that, in most situations, you won’t really be powering 60-watt light bulbs for hours on end. You’ll be charging phones and laptops for an hour here or there, cooling a fridge that kicks on and off every once in a while, using power tools in short bursts, and whatnot.

Power stations are rated in charge cycles, not years. Jackery rates its v2 Explorers for 4,000 cycles before they drop to 70 percent of their original capacity, for example. How many years that adds up to depends on how often you drain and refill the battery, and on storing it within the manufacturer’s temperature range. The best-designed power stations are pretty sturdy, with few to no moving parts, so they should likely keep kicking for a long time, provided that you care for them properly. I’ve been pretty rough with a few of mine, and they show no signs of stopping.

Yes and no. While it’s absolutely possible to power your house with solar power, you’re unlikely to do so with a portable solar generator unless you use several at once while limiting your power usage. High-capacity picks such as the Bluetti Apex 300 and EcoFlow Delta 3 Ultra Plus come closest when paired with extra batteries, but how long they last depends on what you run, how much solar you can add, and the weather. Running house circuits, rather than plugging appliances straight into the station, requires a transfer switch or interlock installed by an electrician. Never backfeed power through a wall outlet.

We’re living in a “golden age” for portable solar generators. When I was a kid, and my family was playing around with solar gear while camping in the ‘90s, the technology couldn’t charge many devices, so it wasn’t all that practical.

By contrast, the solar generators I’ve recommended here are incredibly useful. I’ve relied on them to power my work and day-to-day needs while road-tripping nationwide. They’re also great when the power goes out. When a windstorm cut the power at my house for a couple of days, I was still working, watching my stories, and keeping the lights on.

We haven’t even scratched the surface in terms of the potential offered by portable, reliable, renewable, relatively affordable power. What we can do now is already incredible. The potential for what may come next, though, is even more exciting.

#4633. New Jersey is putting 10 MW of community solar on warehouse roofs

Warehouse roofs are prime real estate for solar, and Faropoint is putting more of that underused space to work in New Jersey. The industrial property owner has started construction on the first of 16 community solar projects totaling more than 10 megawatts (MW).

First up is a 1.6 MW rooftop array at 19-05 Nevins Road in Fair Lawn. Another 15 projects, totaling about 8.5 MW, have been accepted into New Jersey’s Community Solar Energy Program, and nine are already cleared to start construction.

That’s more solar going onto buildings that are already there, with participating households set to get savings on their electricity bills.

Large warehouse roofs offer something solar developers need: lots of flat space. Putting panels up there gives the same building the job of generating electricity without taking up additional land.

Faropoint specializes in industrial properties used for local deliveries and distribution. “Utilizing previously unused portions of our buildings allows us to support the communities where we invest,” said Brian Nave, Faropoint’s vice president of asset management and renewable energy.

Faropoint and its independent solar adviser, SolarKal, expect the 16 projects to generate around 12.7 million kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity annually once they’re operating. They estimate the portfolio will avoid about 8,500 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions a year.

Faropoint says at least half of each project’s capacity will be reserved for low- and moderate-income households. New Jersey’s program requires a minimum of 51%.

Excellent. There are so many warehouses around here, it always baffled me that they weren't all covered with solar panels. Next we gotta get to work on all the parking lots.

Faropoint and SolarKal have not yet announced completion dates, subscription prices, or enrollment details for their New Jersey warehouse roof community solar portfolio.

#4632. Why Cancer Biomarker Testing Is Personal for Mark-Paul Gosselaar

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.

Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.

“Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline. “We are constantly aware of new technologies.”

Having seen people in his life navigate cancer diagnoses, Gosselaar is now raising awareness about the role of biomarker testing in cancer treatment through his partnership with AstraZeneca and its Meet Your Mark campaign.

The campaign aims to educate people facing cancer diagnoses and their loved ones about how biomarker testing may help doctors make more informed, personalized treatment decisions. It also encourages patients to discuss testing with their healthcare teams.

“Biomarkers may tell doctors the specific type of cancer present and if targeted therapies or immunotherapy might help,” Mark Socinski, MD, oncologist and Executive Medical Director of the AdventHealth Cancer Institute, told Healthline.

He explained that biomarkers are typically genes or proteins that doctors measure through blood or tissue tests. They are used to help guide treatment in numerous diseases but are especially powerful tools in many types of cancer.

“They help decode why cancers behave differently, even when two people have the same cancer type,” said Socinski. “However, while biomarker testing provides useful information, it does not guarantee a specific outcome.”

Despite those limitations, Socinski sees promise in the shift from one-size-fits-all cancer treatment to care tailored to each patient’s specific cancer characteristics.

“Biomarker testing does play a critical role here, and it is important for people to be aware of the potential benefits,” Socinski said. “It may help change the course of a person’s treatment journey.”

Gosselaar hopes that greater awareness of biomarker testing can help people facing a cancer diagnosis feel more informed about their treatment options.

“A lot of the time, when a loved one or someone who has been diagnosed with cancer [it can] feel like your world is in a tailspin,” he said. “I wanted to get the word out for anyone who’s going through a cancer diagnosis, or a caretaker, to know that biomarker testing is an option, because even though two cancers are similar, their tumors can act very differently and biomarker testing may help the medical expert with more personalized treatment.”

As part of the campaign, Gosselaar took part in a commercial, something he hadn’t done since before his days on “Saved by the Bell.”

“This was the first time that I actually had to be on set and not be a character; I had to be me talking about this very serious issue,” he said.

While it was a challenging experience, he said it was also fulfilling.

“I enjoyed the process, and to be able to use my platform to be able to spread the word; it means a lot to me,” he said. “I’m very selective of the things that I want to attach myself to, and this seemed like the right fit.”

He particularly enjoyed recreating Zack Morris’s signature “timeout” gesture from “Saved by the Bell,” which allowed his character to freeze time and speak directly to the camera.

“Using something from the past that was such a symbolic gesture to so many people of my generation that are now my age and possibly going through [cancer] or knowing someone who’s going through [cancer to] direct them to [this campaign], means a lot,” he said.

Beyond his efforts to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing, Gosselaar is equally focused on taking care of his own health.

Getting quality sleep is one of his top priorities. He sleeps on a high-tech mattress that monitors sleep stages, heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiratory rate. He also uses a biometric health and fitness tracker, prioritizes healthy eating, and uses saunas and red light therapy.

“We do everything that we possibly can, but I’m less about longevity and more about just living a healthy lifestyle,” Gosselaar said. “I want to continue doing the things that I’ve done since I was a child…without feeling held back by my health.”

As he embraces his 50s, he said he’d like to live a long life for his children and future grandchildren. He started taking his health seriously in his 40s after undergoing shoulder surgery.

“[It] really made me realize [that] all the damage I had done in my 20s and 30s sort of adds up later in life, and that’s probably something that I would tell the younger me… to preserve a little bit more and take [an] approach that recovery is just as important as the workout because I did not use my recovery very well; it was not a priority for me,” said Gosselaar.

He also makes time for himself every day. He said doing so makes him a better person and more able to care for his wife and four children.

“[It’s] something that I believe in; that I need to do something for myself before I can do something for someone else. Or if I do something for someone else, then I have to equalize that by doing something for me,” he said.

Daily physical activity also helps support his mental well-being.

“I need to do something where I challenge myself, and it could be as simple as a walk. It could be as simple as just getting outside and lifting something heavy [or] taking bags of groceries and taking the long way into your house,” Gosselaar said.

“Like challenging yourself with picking up things, you know, taking backpacks from the car from your kids and seeing if you can carry three in one hand…or going into the gym and spending an hour in the gym, or 30 minutes, or just moving.”

When he’s in the sauna, he works on breathing and clearing his thoughts.

“Some people need to meditate, some people need to talk to somebody. I encourage all of that because I think all of that helps,” he said.

“I’ve done them all. I’ve done the cold plunging, I’ve done all that stuff…some of it works, and some of it doesn’t; it’s whatever you believe in. So I just encourage people to stay healthy and move, get outside, and help other people.”

#4630. Segway launches new electric motorcycle that’s so safe it has seatbelts

Segway came to EICMA this year with a surprisingly broad lineup of new electric motorcycles, ranging from high-performance concepts to off-road machines. But perhaps the most interesting of the bunch is also the one that looks the least like a conventional motorcycle or scooter.

Meet the Segway X Cruiser, an electric two-wheeler that takes motorcycle safety so seriously that it has a roll cage and seatbelts.

Or at least, those are among the configurations Segway is showing as it develops the new machine for production.

The X Cruiser is Segway’s attempt to bring more automotive-style protection to a single-track vehicle, essentially asking how much of a car’s safety envelope can be wrapped around a motorcycle without adding another pair of wheels.

From the looks of things, the answer is quite a lot.

Segway says the X Cruiser’s design was informed by automotive crash scenarios, with cage and semi-cage structures, four-direction collision protection, staged energy absorption, and seatbelt restraints intended to improve rider protection. It also gets active safety features including standard blind spot detection and lane change warning.

The company showed several ways that basic idea can be configured, ranging from a more conventional partially enclosed scooter-like setup to versions with significantly more structure surrounding the rider. One of the most striking configurations uses a heavily bolstered race-car-style seat and seatbelt along with protective framing around the rider, while another adds a roof for even more enclosure.

It’s a fascinating approach because motorcycles have traditionally relied largely on the rider wearing the protection. Helmets, jackets, gloves, boots and sometimes airbag vests form the safety system, while the motorcycle itself generally offers little physical protection during a crash.

The X Cruiser effectively flips part of that equation by building some of the protective structure into the vehicle itself.

There’s an important caveat here, though. Segway specifically notes that its descriptions refer to the vehicle’s current design and equipment and do not mean it has completed automotive-style crash certification. Final equipment and certification will depend on individual markets, so it sounds like the company is holding short of making any major certification claims. Still though, it’s easy to see how having what is effectively a racing seat and roll cage surrounding the rider could seriously contribute to better protection in a crash. Just remember to keep your hands and feet within the vehicle at all times.

And unlike plenty of wild EICMA showpieces, this one isn’t merely destined to live under convention-center spotlights. Segway says the X Cruiser has a confirmed mass-production plan, with launches planned for China and Europe between 2027 and 2028. There’s no US availability announcement yet.

Underneath all that protective hardware is a fairly serious electric touring platform. Segway is using its CTB (cell-to-body) battery integration to help improve structural rigidity and battery packaging, with the company targeting nearly 200 km (124 miles) of range.

European versions are expected to feature 4.5 kW Type 2 AC charging, while the Chinese version will offer optional higher-power DC fast charging. The bike rolls on 15-inch front and 14-inch rear wheels wearing Michelin City Grip tires, and riders get a 10.25-inch TFT display along with an optional 55-liter electrically operated top box.

Interestingly, the X Cruiser also incorporates certain two-wheeler intellectual property and know-how licensed from BMW Group, though Segway stresses that it is responsible for the vehicle’s development, integration, validation, production and certification.

The X Cruiser may be the weirdest – and thus perhaps the most interesting – of Segway’s EICMA debuts, but it was far from alone.

The company also unveiled the Segway Orca Concept, a futuristic high-performance electric maxi-scooter concept built around an 800V electrical architecture and a nearly 20 kWh battery.

Segway is targeting up to 300 km (186 miles) of range, a 0-100 km/h (0-62 mph) time of 4.5 seconds, and the ability to add 200 km (124 miles) of range in 20 minutes. The concept also features front and rear multi-link suspension, electronically controlled multi-mode damping and a battery-integrated CTB chassis. Those figures are engineering targets rather than promised production specifications, and Segway currently describes the Orca strictly as a concept.

Its a BMW C1 reborn as electric! They were a bit of a cult thing, but underpowered for the weight. Never made it to the USA.

The biggest benefit is not really safety, its comfort.

Then there’s Segway’s expanding X Series, which moves the focus away from urban riding and toward dirt. The lineup includes the Xaber X1000 and Xaber 350, along with different Xaber 300 variants for the US and European markets. Segway is also partnering with Michelin for its Dakar Rally Factory Team, using the brutal rally environment as a real-world development and validation platform for electric off-road motorcycles.

Taken together, it’s quite the showing from a company whose name many people still associate primarily with those funny two-wheeled self-balancing machines from the early 2000s.

Segway has already expanded heavily into electric scooters, e-bikes, go-karts and powersports vehicles. Now it seems increasingly serious about becoming an electric motorcycle company as well.

And if motorcycles with roll cages, roofs and seatbelts are part of that future, things could get pretty interesting… pretty quickly!

#4629. Mercedes-Benz Asks: What If We Put Screens in a Car’s Windows, Too?

New window display technology could unlock the opportunity to include even more screens in Mercedes automobiles.

If there’s a space to insert a screen, the folks at Mercedes-Benz will find it. And turns out, the carmaker’s engineers have found what they consider the next frontier to be conquered: your car’s windows. On Tuesday, Mercedes released previews of two new types of window displays, one called Intelligent Display in Glass and the other named Holographic Display.

The “Intelligent Display in Glass” essentially puts LED display elements directly into the vehicle windows. Why? Mercedes says warning symbols or traffic-related information could be displayed on the rear window to warn those behind you. One might presume brake lights do the trick of letting folks know you’re slowing down, but the examples Mercedes shows are much more specific as to the reason you’re slowing down; the glass can project the symbol of a car accident, pedestrian crossing, or all sorts of other things.

Our favorite is the text that simply reads “KEEP DISTANCE.” Could that potentially just enrage a tailgater even more? Sure, but it’s also objectively funny to have your car tell people behind you to back off.

Mercedes says it’s investigating two different LED technologies for this application. Mini LEDs are best-suited to larger displays in the rear window; meanwhile, Micro LEDs could be used on smaller areas to show animations, thanks to their higher resolution capabilities.

Examples of Micro LEDs in action are shown in the side window screens, where the car can display messages to its driver like battery charge status or a simple “goodbye” as you walk away. In both cases, when no content is displayed, Mercedes says the display elements laminated into the glass composite “remain almost invisible.” The “almost” there gives us some pause, so we’ll have to see it in person in order to make a judgement.

The other tech Mercedes previewed is the Holographic Display, which looks a bit like a HUD on steroids. A projector in the instrument panel would project content onto a new windshield that uses a special transparent film laminated into the glass. Mercedes says the display will be viewable only at specific viewing angles—the driver wouldn’t be able to see what’s projected in front of the passenger, and vice versa. The carmaker says this means the passenger could be watching a film projected onto the windshield, while the driver is shown navigation information.

In pictures, at least it’s better than a HUD in that the display looks like a projection you might see in a home theater setup. You get full color and a sharp image, though the examples that the carmaker showcases aren’t exactly too enticing, being images of Mercedes vehicles and the weather.

Just like the other displays shown in this preview, Mercedes says all of these ideas simply demonstrate potential future approaches. None of them are likely to end up in a production car any time soon, as they’re all currently under development. That said, now would be the time to sound off and let Mercedes know if any of the above is something you’d want in a car one day ... or not.

BYD launched the new Seal 07 in China, where it starts at around $23,000. It’s about the size of a Toyota Camry, but brings a surprising amount of tech and premium features for the money.

After introducing the updated first-generation Seal 07 in March, BYD launched the second-gen model on Thursday.

The second-generation Seal 07, which BYD calls the “new choice for a class-leading luxury experience,” is available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains.

BYD offers five variants, including two PHEVs and three EVs, starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

The new Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery, providing a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).

It comes standard with a single rear-mounted electric motor producing up to 328 hp (245 kW) and 269 lb-ft (365 Nm) of torque, which BYD says enables it to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 5.5 seconds.

All plug-in hybrid variants use BYD’s latest DM-i system, which features a 1.5L turbocharged engine with 154 hp (115 kW) and a 214 hp (160 kW) front electric motor.

The Seal 07 debuts BYD’s Smart Ecosystem 2.0, including “Diva,” a smartwatch that can interact with the vehicle and let drivers manage functions remotely.

Higher-priced models offer BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, with a roof-mounted LiDAR available as an option. The setup provides safety and convenience features such as Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.

BYD is offering a limited-time “Super trade-in price” promo, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the new Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.

#4627. Tokyo police consider using AI to reconstruct traffic accidents

Published Nov 5, 2026 11:07 AM EST

One law enforcement agency in Japan reportedly wants to make something normally confined to sci-fi crime thrillers a reality: interactive, AI-powered reconstructions of real-world accidents. According to The Japan Times, Tokyo’s Metropolitan Department is developing a system that combines AI with security camera footage and 3D spatial data captured by camera-equipped mapping vehicles to digitally reconstruct traffic accidents. Investigators using the tool would reportedly be able to measure vehicle speeds and distances on a screen and replay the event in simulation from multiple perspectives, including overhead or even through the eyes of a nearby driver or pedestrian.

That’s the goal, at least. Details about how this proposed system will actually work remain sparse, though the report says that the police plan to begin testing in June 2027 and potentially launch full operations in January 2028. In theory, digital reconstructions could reduce the need for labor-intensive physical, on-site inspections (the current approach) which can close off roads for ours and lead to traffic jams.

However, AI reconstructions bring risks of their own, especially if they rely on generative AI tools that are prone to hallucinating fabricated data. In the United States  and elsewhere, courts are struggling to reign in examples of inaccurate, AI-generated court filings and police reports. The use of AI-enhanced video and audio and even deepfake clones presented in trials are also forcing the legal system to reevaluate how it treats algorithm-altered evidence.

As far as we can tell, the Tokyo police proposal would be the first systematic use of an AI reconstruction for traffic assessments. In 2024, law enforcement in Pune, India, east of Mumbai, reportedly considered using an AI-enabled “digital reconstruction” to analyze a high profile drunk driving incident that killed two pedestrians. But it’s unclear whether that system was ever actually realized or used in court.

Researchers have been exploring the underlying technology for such a system for years. In July, a team from the Technical University of Munich and the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office in Germany showed off an AI system they say is capable of compiling thousands of photographers from a crime scene to create a digital reconstruction. In that case, the team said the system could automatically identify and classify objects in the scene. Investigators could then virtually go in and query the 3D crime scene to try and collect and analyze evidence long after the actual event occurred.

Meanwhile, researchers at Hasselt University in Belgium, are also in the early stage of developing a tool aiming to use multimodal language models for digital reconstructions which they say could aid law enforcement and insurers.

Generative AI tools are also creating new headaches for the legal system. Hundreds of lawyers around the globe have been sanctioned by courts for filling legal briefs with bogus, hallucinated case law. In June, a judge in Mississippi canceled a civil trial’s proceedings after all four lawyers on opposing sides of the case were caught citing a fake, AI-generated court filing. And citations are not the only issue. A growing number of police departments in the U.S. are using AI tools to analyze evidence and draft police reports, which the American Civil Liberty Union warns “removes important human elements from police procedures.”

At least partially AI-generated evidence, like the kind that many result from a digital reconstitution, has already appeared in some legal proceedings. In 2024, a Washington State judge overseeing a murder case barred the defendant’s lawyers from introducing cellphone footage that had been digitally enhanced using AI software. According to court filings at the time, the judge in that case worried that admitting that AI- enhanced footage could “lead to a confusion of the issue and muddling of eyewitness testimony.”

The core tension here, and with other uses of AI as evidence, is whether or not the AI system can be trusted to accurately reflect reality. An AI system reconstructing traffic scenes, though potentially  less higher stages than a murder trial, may nonetheless face similar headwinds.

Whether you’re dealing with deep-seated pet hair, stubborn crumbs, or layers of dust, this vacuum does its job with ease. There was a noticeable difference even after just one go-over on the floor mat. The Vac N Blo never felt like it struggled, wherever we were vacuuming.

When you need to dry your car or blast grit out of vents, the blower function is just as powerful, making it a true two-in-one garage essential. I used this setting to blow the bits of dirt and gravel right out of the garage door.

It also allows you the option to attach wheels, making it even easier to maneuver. In this case, I attached the shoulder strap and had it move with me as I worked my way around the mats and car. It’s also a very sleek design—it looked sharp in the garage and stood out not just in performance but also in aesthetics.

Beyond its power, the all-metal construction gives it a level of durability you won’t find in typical car vacuums. The long hose and multiple attachments make tackling every inch of your interior easy, turning a once-dreaded task into a precision operation. If you want a vacuum that’ll deliver professional-level results, the Metrovac Vac N Blo is the one to get.

The DetailVac is the smallest on the list, and it was also the easiest to work with. It plugged right into the Boxster’s 12-volt outlet and, at only three pounds, was easy to maneuver. The 16-foot cord is long enough to accommodate a bigger vehicle with multiple seats or crevices. Overall, it does what it states but doesn’t excel.

While it picked up most of the dust and dirt on the floor mats, it left behind pet fur and debris. The vacuum includes three attachments that are helpful in harder-to-reach spots: The crevice tool worked well, but the brush tool didn’t do much for puppy fur. A flexible connection hose also acts as an extended hose, but it seemed to diminish the suction power when added. It’s not as powerful as the others we tested, which makes sense given its size.

I liked that an additional air filter was included. Depending on how often you use the vacuum, the filters can last up to six months without needing a change, but it’s nice that an extra one is provided.

Overall, the DetailVac is convenient and great for quick cleanups or accidents. I think it would be especially helpful if you have kids.

The Bissell Garage Pro Wall-Mounted Wet/Dry Vacuum is for anyone serious about keeping their car and garage clean. Mounted on your wall with a 32-foot hose, it delivers strong 12-amp suction to tackle dirt and wet spills. There’s a blower option, perfect for drying off a freshly washed Porsche, which I did with stellar results.

Even at its size, assembly was simple. Once it’s together, it performs at the level you’d expect from a professional detailing station. This is the best pick if you have the room and use a vacuum in your garage often. It’s a full-service garage vacuum built to take a beating and deliver strong suction for any surface of your vehicle.

What also sets it apart is its auto-tool kit, which includes attachments—crevice tools, upholstery brushes, and a wet nozzle for moisture cleanup—for every cleaning scenario.

Whether you’re an obsessive detailer or just want a cleaner ride, the Garage Pro delivers. It is powerful, versatile, and a worthwhile addition to any garage.

Adam’s Polishes Wall-Mounted Vacuum packs a lot of power for a smaller unit. I quickly understood why most people use the wall-mount option; not only does it help keep the 30-foot hose out of the way, but it also helps keep your garage organized. If I had mounted this, the hose probably would’ve been less cumbersome to maneuver. Drilling holes in our space to mount several vacuums was not an option, but we did our best to re-create this real-world scenario. Assembly was a bit of a struggle—especially getting the central hose in—but I might not have used enough force initially. My advice would be to use all your strength; I promise you won’t break it.

The suction is decent, with 120 volts of power, but the attachments really help this vacuum shine: steel telescoping wand, bare-floor tool, snake wand, crevice tool, elongated dust brush, and upholstery tool. They make this vacuum even more versatile, allowing you to tackle everything from floor mats to delicate surfaces efficiently.

Using this vacuum was genuinely satisfying, like power-washing your interior with suction. Adam’s did indeed get the job done fast, and had it been wall-mounted, I think I would’ve seen its overall appeal, since using the hose would likely be more manageable. Adam’s Polishes Wall-Mounted Vacuum is worth every penny for those who love organization.

The Shark StainForce isn’t your typical car vacuum, and that’s precisely why we wanted to include it. Rather than tackling loose dirt, this cordless spot cleaner focuses on stubborn oil stains, soda spills, and odors embedded in your car’s carpeting.

There’s a three-step cleaning process involved, but it’s well worth the extra work. Spray the affected area with Shark’s dual-activated cleaning solution, scrub with the included attachment, and use the vacuum’s suction to extract the mess. The dual-chamber formula mixes when sprayed, helping break down stains without requiring any measuring or extra preparation. Two attachments, including a crevice tool, make it easier to reach tight spaces around seats and other interior surfaces.

Weighing under three pounds, the StainForce is easy to maneuver, and its cordless design eliminates the hassle of finding an outlet. The included storage caddy keeps everything organized between cleanups.

There are a few limitations. Battery life topped out at approximately 20 minutes when we tested (so it still works fine for spot cleaning). Also, you’ll need to purchase Shark’s own cleaning solution when the included supply runs out.

For drivers regularly battling coffee spills, muddy footprints, or pet accidents, the StainForce offers a convenient, targeted cleaning solution.

A high-quality vacuum cleaner can make all the difference for keeping your car’s interior spotless. Unlike household vacuums, car-specific models are designed to tackle heavier debris in tight spaces. However, with so many options available, choosing the right one can be overwhelming. It’s important to consider key features that affect performance and convenience to make an informed decision.

Three of the most crucial factors to evaluate are suction power, which determines how effectively the vacuum picks up dirt; attachments and accessories, which help clean hard-to-reach areas; and the power source, which impacts portability and run time.

Understanding these features will help you find a vacuum that best suits your needs, whether you prioritize strong suction for deep cleaning, versatile tools for detail work, or the malleability of a hose. Let’s dive into these essential features to ensure you choose the right car vacuum cleaner for the job.

Suction power is the most critical factor in a car vacuum because vehicle interiors can become a nightmare with everything we drag in and out of them. Unlike home carpets, car surfaces are filled with a million little spaces, textured upholstery, and stubborn floor mats that anything you can think of clings to. A vacuum with weak suction won’t be able to extract dirt that’s ground into these surfaces, leaving your car looking only half clean. Not ideal.

Additionally, higher suction power means faster, more efficient cleaning. Instead of repeatedly going over the same spot, a strong vacuum gets the job done in fewer passes, saving you time and effort. It also helps tackle heavier things such as leaves, sand, or pebbles. If you take your car’s cleanliness seriously (or don’t want to spend forever vacuuming), a high-powered vacuum is the way to go.

Attachments and accessories are essential in a car vacuum because car interiors are full of tight spaces and tricky surfaces that a standard nozzle can’t handle. Unlike home vacuums, which deal with flat carpets and open areas, a car vacuum must navigate between seats, air vents, and cup holders, all of which require specialized tools.

For example, a crevice tool helps reach between and along door panels, while a brush attachment is perfect for loosening dust from dashboards. Wide nozzles quickly work on large areas like a trunk, and wet/dry tools handle accidents before they become permanent stains. The right attachments don’t just make cleaning easier; they ensure you’re getting every last crumb out of your ride, leaving it truly spotless.

The power source of a car vacuum determines its suction strength, mobility, and convenience. Corded (AC-powered) vacuums offer the strongest suction but require an outlet and may limit movement. Cordless (battery-powered) models provide maximum portability for quick cleanups but often have weaker suction and limited run time.

Vacuums that plug into a car’s 12-volt outlet are great for on-the-go use but generally lack the power of AC models. Choosing the right type depends on your needs, such as going corded for power, cordless for convenience, or 12-volt for in-car accessibility.

The ThisWorx portable car vacuum routinely came up as the one to avoid. Its low suction didn’t do much, leaving most of the dirt and dust behind. While it is inexpensive, you do indeed get what you pay for.

The same goes for generic no-name vacuums on Amazon. While they are more affordable, they are also unreliable and often break within months of purchase.

We focused on suction power, attachments, and ease of use for this test. Using substantially dirty floor mats as our starting point, we taped them off to determine which vacuum was the most powerful. These mats were full of dirt, dust, pebbles, and dog fur; they were pretty much littered with what you might encounter in your vehicle. This strategy helped us quickly determine which vacuums were up to the task.

Our garage in New Brunswick, New Jersey, was the ideal backdrop for this test. Not only was it still dirty from summer trips, it also allowed me to spread out the old and very used floor mats I’d be using. While this test focused on how effectively the vacuums would clean up cars, a happy surprise was that they also cleaned the garage.

For this test, we reached out to pros to see what products they prefer. After determining fan favorites, digging around forums, and connecting with detailers we’ve worked with in the past, we devised a list of items to review. (You know you’re headed in the right direction when you hear the same brand or product come up multiple times.) This is how we arrived at Chemical Guys, Adam’s, Bissell, and Shark—solid and reliable brands. Metrovac popped up in my digging as a reliable shop vac in a popular Reddit group (r/AutoDetailing). They weren’t wrong.

We didn’t look at handheld car vacuums in this test. While they’re tops for convenience, they would be a separate category to investigate, given their variety. We did keep convenience in mind when picking the units we wanted to focus on, but this test was done with serious garage owners and car enthusiasts in mind.

When we reviewed the Car+Boat from Dyson, we were immensely impressed at how well the mini-vac lived up to its brand’s legacy. With legendary suction power, the Dyson was as much a revelation for car lovers as the company’s larger vacuums were for homeowners all those years ago.

Portable, lightweight, and affordable. What more could you want in a car vac? With a 20-volt MAX Li-ion battery and extra-long crevice tool, it’s as great for the car as it is around the house.

Looking for a little more power than a portable cordless vacuum can provide? Pick up this mini-utility shop vac from Armor All. It’s far more convenient than lugging around a larger shop vac, has a washable filter, and doubles as a blower.

When choosing a car or garage vacuum, size and capacity are crucial factors that impact performance and convenience. A vacuum with anywhere from two to six gallons of capacity is usually sufficient for car detailing, providing enough volume for typical debris while remaining lightweight and portable. Smaller vacuums are easier to maneuver inside a car and can be stored conveniently in a garage or trunk.

A 10-plus-gallon shop vacuum is better for garage use or frequent heavy-duty cleaning. These larger models can handle bigger messes, including sawdust, metal shavings, and wet spots, without requiring frequent emptying. They also typically feature more powerful motors for increased suction. However, they take up more storage space and may be less portable. If you need a balance between power and maneuverability, a mid-size vacuum can provide strong suction without being too bulky.

While a regular household vacuum might seem convenient for cleaning your car or garage, it often lacks the necessary power, durability, and specialized attachments for effective cleaning in these environments. Household vacuums are designed primarily for indoor surfaces such as carpets and hardwood floors, meaning they may struggle to pick up messes commonly found in cars and garages. Their shorter hoses and bulkier designs can make it challenging to reach tight spaces.

Dedicated car vacuums and shop vacuums are better suited for these tasks, offering more powerful suction, longer hoses, and attachments specifically designed for automotive cleaning. These vacuums are built with durability, often featuring rugged designs that can withstand dust, moisture, and rough handling in a garage setting. While household vacuums may work in a pinch for light cleaning, investing in a purpose-built car or garage vacuum ensures more efficient cleaning and a longer-lasting machine.

HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters are essential when purchasing a car or garage vacuum, especially if you are concerned about air quality. Standard vacuum filters may struggle to trap fine particles such as dust, pollen, pet dander, and mold spores, which can get released back into the air during cleaning.

HEPA filters, however, are designed to capture at least 99.97 percent of particles, making them highly effective at reducing allergens and airborne contaminants. This is particularly beneficial if you suffer from allergies.

For car and garage cleaning, a HEPA or high-efficiency filtration system can also help keep your vehicle’s interior and your garage workspace cleaner by preventing fine dust from resettling. While HEPA-filtered vacuums may be slightly more expensive, they offer significant benefits for maintaining a healthier environment.

#4625. GLP-1s May Help Lower Diabetes, Heart Risks Better Than Standard Prevention

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 drugs are more effective in helping prevent type 2 diabetes than the commonly prescribed medication metformin, according to a new study.

Researchers said GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro were more likely to reduce blood sugar to healthy levels in people with prediabetes and obesity.

They added that people prescribed GLP-1 medications had a lower risk of progressing from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

The researchers noted that GLP-1 users also had a lower risk of death from any cause as well as fewer heart attacks, strokes, and heart failure events compared with metformin users.

“The great news with prediabetes is that it’s still possible to reverse the progression of the disease,” said Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, MD, a study author and research fellow in cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, in a press release. “This research may add to the case for considering GLP-1 medications earlier for certain patients, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes.”

Serra noted that metformin still remains an effective treatment for people with prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.

“This is less about replacing one medication with another and more about discussing additional options with specific patients,” he said.

The researchers presented their findings at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

David Cutler, MD, a family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, wasn’t involved in the study, but said the findings were “quite impressive.”

“It elevates the comfort of prescribing GLP-1 drugs as a front-line treatment,” he told Healthline.

Robert Eckel, MD, a former president of the American Heart Association who was likewise not involved in the study, agrees the research provides more options for patients and prescribers.

“GLP-1s provide another option for prevention, perhaps as an add-on therapy. However, costs and access to these medications are important factors,” said Eckel, an endocrinologist at the University of Colorado School of Medicine, in the press release.

For their study, the researchers analyzed the medical records of 256,000 adults in the United States with prediabetes and obesity. About 76% of the subjects were women, and the average age of the participants was 52.

About half of those studied were taking GLP-1 drugs with the active ingredient semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, or dulaglutide.

The other half had been prescribed metformin, a medication used to help manage blood sugar levels in adults and some children with type 2 diabetes by decreasing glucose production in the liver, reducing glucose absorption from food, and improving the body’s insulin sensitivity.

The researchers reported that the people in the study who were taking GLP-1 drugs had a 1.5 times higher chance of reversing high blood sugar to healthy levels compared to people who were using metformin.

The researchers also noted that GLP-1 medication users had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death from any cause.

They added that GLP-1 medications were associated with 15% fewer heart attacks, 20% fewer strokes, 25% fewer cases of heart failure, and 8% fewer cases of atrial fibrillation (AFib), a common type of irregular heartbeat.

The researchers cautioned that their study is observational and, therefore, cannot prove a cause-and-effect relationship. They also noted they relied on prescription records, so the frequency and dosage at which patients took their medication was not reflected.

In addition, the GLP-1 drugs were grouped together, so individual differences between medications were not considered.

Eckel said in the news release that the benefits for people taking GLP-1 drugs were probably mainly due to weight loss. Eckel noted that the research results open up a wide range of possibilities.

“This is an important finding because the GLP-1 receptor agonists are commonly used today and this is a population that in the transition from prediabetes to diabetes are at increasing risk for cardiovascular disease,” Eckel said in a taped interview alongside the study findings.

Cutler pointed out that several GLP-1 drugs also target blood sugar levels and insulin production. They could be effective in people with prediabetes who don’t have weight management issues.

Cutler noted that these people, however, might be reluctant to take GLP-1 drugs because they may not be experiencing symptoms of their prediabetes but could develop side effects with the medications.

“They would not be getting any immediate benefits,” Cutler said. He added that metformin, which was first used clinically in 1958, remains an effective alternative. “It’s been proven safe, effective, and it’s very cheap,” Cutler said.

It’s estimated that 40 million people in the United States have diabetes, with more than 90% of those cases being type 2 diabetes, a chronic condition characterized by high blood glucose levels that results from the body’s ineffective response to insulin or insufficient insulin production.

It’s also estimated that 115 million adults in the United States have prediabetes, a condition in which a person has higher-than-normal blood sugar levels but not high enough to be diagnosed as type 2 diabetes.

Around 5–10% of people with prediabetes develop diabetes every year. More broadly, up to 70% of people with prediabetes eventually develop diabetes.

Medication is sometimes prescribed for people with type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Lifestyle changes can help reverse type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as prevent the progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes.

Cutler said the lifestyle changes needed to prevent type 2 diabetes are pretty clear.

“The most important thing for people with prediabetes to know is they should lose weight, reduce their carbs, exercise daily and, if that doesn’t work, then consider medication,” he said.
